explanation: The moderator raises whether general and personal feedback should be collected together or separately, reflecting concern about how feedback should be structured so that it is clear and usable.
quote: do you think it's good to have them both in one form, or separately?

explanation: Effective use of feedback is framed as the University acknowledging student concerns and reporting back on whether changes will be made or why current practice will remain. This makes the feedback process visible and transparent to students.
quote: “we would like hear that just maybe next year it will be changed and that they thought about it, or maybe give us some sort of justification of why they’re doing it this way… gets back to us explaining why it stays the same way, or what they're going to do about it.”

explanation: The student emphasises that feedback should not be a one-way submission but part of an ongoing discussion, where students know their feedback has been considered even if change is not immediate.
quote: “i would like to see some kind of dialogue, somehow discussion that happens and occurs, i think it's important for students to know that our feedback is being discussed”

explanation: Students describe feedback as effective when it identifies a specific issue in course design and leads to a concrete response, either a change in future provision or a clear rationale for maintaining the current approach.
quote: “if we've kind of like raised an issue with a certain part of the course that something seems kind of illogical… maybe next year it will be changed… or what they're going to do about it.”

explanation: The student recognises that institutional change may be slow, but still values evidence that feedback is being processed and considered within the system.
quote: “change is something that happens very slowly… i don't expect them like next year that they immediately change the course name… but i would like to see some kind of dialogue”

explanation: The student describes not receiving feedback directly from the course organisers and only hearing about the issue later through their personal tutor in the following semester, suggesting feedback was delayed and less useful because it was not provided close to the relevant course experience.
quote: “i didn’t hear back from any of the organisers i just heard from my pt while we were like talking about it the next semester”

explanation: The speaker identifies the gender and ethnicity of course staff, but this segment does not provide information about the quality, content, timing, usability, or consistency of feedback.
quote: “mine it was actually for a gender course by merrill kenny, who's female and white and then the other course organiser not sure of her ethnicity, she's brown. also female”

explanation: The student describes being invited to ask questions or book time with finance, but there were no appointment slots available, making institutional guidance inaccessible and not practically usable.
quote: “before the whole school year started, they were like, oh, if you have any questions or anything, just reserve a time with the finance department. tell me why there were no time slots, nothing.”

explanation: Students report long waits to contact finance and delayed replies about housing support, suggesting feedback or institutional responses were not provided quickly enough to be useful.
quote: “even the phone lines we've just got... i've been on hold for like an hour.” / “they let me know two weeks later being like, oh, sorry, like you can apply for long term accommodation.”

explanation: The student received finance-related information that appeared incorrect or unclear, particularly around fee status, making the communication difficult to trust or act upon.
quote: “they’re letting me pay uk fees at the moment as a part time student, as a resident… that's an interesting thing to see on an email, because i'm not from here.”

explanation: The student was advised to contact finance and later offered a housing route, but the proposed solution involved a very long wait and did not address the immediate problem caused by the university process.
quote: “you should contact finance if you don't want this to affect the situation” / “you can apply for long term accommodation. but it's probably going to take a minimum of nine months because the waitlist.”

explanation: A student frames the issue as the university failing to listen to complaints despite students paying for the service; this is more about institutional dissatisfaction than feedback on student learning.
quote: “we are paying customers. they're supposed to, you know, hear our complaints… we're not getting what we're paying for.”

explanation: The student associates smaller class sizes with more positive lecturer interactions and greater willingness to provide help, suggesting feedback/support is easier to access in more personalised settings.
quote: “most positive ones within a smaller class usually… optional econ courses which is just like, less than 20 or 30 people… the lecture is like, they're like, awesome”

explanation: The lecturer responded to a problem by managing the situation and offering extra help, reflecting feedback/support that is available when needed and close to the issue occurring.
quote: “the lecturer, like, kind of managed the situation quite well. and they said, they can provide, like extra help”

explanation: The student contrasts helpful lecturers with others who avoid dealing with problems or fail to respond, indicating that feedback/support is weakened when staff do not engage with student difficulties.
quote: “some lecturers would like to solve the problems, but some of them just like escape, and just ghosted.”

explanation: The student suggests that when students are more engaged, lecturers are more likely to provide support, implying feedback works as part of an interactive cycle between students and teachers.
quote: “if the students are more engaging, the lecturers would provide...”

explanation: Participants seek clarification about whether the question concerns how student feedback is collected, what feedback students receive, or how feedback is received. This does not provide a substantive view about what makes good feedback, so it is not thematically relevant to the provided feedback-quality themes.
quote: “is it student feedback in terms of like, how we would change how feedback is taken? or is it what feedback we would get?” / “like, how feedback is received?”

explanation: The participant discusses being in a studio and others not coming in, with a side comment about cleaning. This does not relate to qualities of good feedback from the University.
quote: "i'm in a studio so they never come into thing or anything like that, which is good. even though it means i have to clean it."

explanation: The participant describes being overwhelmed by frequent survey requests, leading them to ignore university-related surveys. This concerns participation in surveys rather than feedback to students, so it is not thematically relevant to the provided feedback-quality themes.
quote: “we just get like so many surveys... when someone does try and send a survey around for something like uni related... i personally i just don’t have a look at it.”

code: QR codes perceived as improving response likelihood
explanation: A participant suggests QR codes are more effective than standard survey links because they do not respond to individual surveys. This relates to survey administration and engagement, not the quality or delivery of academic feedback to students.
quote: “that’s why i think the qr codes work a lot better... purely because i don't respond to single surveys.”

explanation: The student expresses frustration that the university is not providing clear details about progress on an issue affecting students. They want observable information about what has been done and how far negotiations have progressed, rather than vague reassurance.
quote: “we’re like mad that students don't know how far the negotiations have gone with one of our concerns saying we just want reassurance.”

code: Desire to be included through ongoing communication
explanation: The student indicates that students want to feel involved and informed as the issue develops. The lack of continuing updates makes them feel excluded from the process.
quote: “students want to take part, but i feel like i'm not taking part… student with the buses are just wondering what's happening”

explanation: The student describes a feedback process where issues are raised repeatedly but no visible action follows, leading students to feel their input has no effect. This reflects the importance of feedback being part of an ongoing cycle in which information is acted upon and leads to adjustment.
quote: “every year they're the same problems with the same courses, the same issues raised and nothing changes… ‘well, it doesn't matter what we say’. because it's still gonna be like, not be acted upon.”

explanation: The student highlights that when changes are not made, staff do not explain why, leaving students unclear about what happened to their feedback. This relates to the need for feedback processes to be transparent and understandable.
quote: “they never even like say like, why it was impossible to change it… we just gonna like a dismiss like, ‘oh yeah, we're going to do something’”

code: No actionable response to student concerns
explanation: The student’s role involves taking student feedback to staff and reporting back what is being done, but they report that most of the time no concrete actions result. This suggests that useful feedback should include specific follow-up actions rather than vague assurances.
quote: “getting back to the feedback from the members of staff to the students so that they know what's being done about the issues. and most of the time, nothing's being done”

explanation: The participant describes school communications as being aimed mainly at staff and not useful or meaningful to students; this does not directly address qualities of academic feedback.
quote: “i think it's like, mostly for staff. yeah it’s, like, so and so wrote a paper... so i’m like, ‘okay...’ when i see it, especially i'm like, i don’t need more of this because it doesn't...”
subtheme: Institutional communication disconnected from student needs

code: Student community associated with union rather than school
explanation: The participant contrasts the visibility of student representative bodies with the school, suggesting SPS is not experienced as the main source of student community. This is not directly about feedback quality.
quote: “compared to like the student union, or student council, or whatever, i think that's much more at the forefront, and the schools are like at the background. so when i think of community, i think of the student council, not sps”

explanation: The participant suggests expanding a student-staff forum beyond programme representatives so that any student with an active issue could attend. This concerns student representation and opportunities for students to raise concerns, rather than the qualities of academic feedback given to students.
quote: "currently the sslc is for the students but program reps, only. so if there's one that every one of ours can also join" ... "it could be like an open forum... students who are more outspoken or have an active problem with the course would like to go"

explanation: The participant identifies a concrete example from a course—lecture notes that were “really well done”—as something staff should examine or emulate. This suggests value in feedback or course guidance being clear enough to serve as an observable model of good practice, although detail is limited.
quote: “things that were done in lecture notes for, one of my courses was really well done that they should look at that.”

explanation: The participant reports that classmates widely shared a negative view about one course, but the extract does not specify what aspect of feedback was problematic or link it clearly to any defined quality of effective feedback.
quote: “for one of my courses, i think like everyone should have the same sort of negative opinion. and it's, it's widely talked about”
subtheme: Collective dissatisfaction without specific feedback detail

explanation: The student indicates that the online discussion space on Learn is difficult to use, limiting its usefulness as a feedback or question-answering channel.
quote: “they’re having a discussion going on learn, which no one can really use so far.”

explanation: The student describes how questions and responses on discussion boards may be misunderstood, suggesting that feedback needs to be communicated clearly and in a way that reduces ambiguity.
quote: “it can be misinterpreted in different ways… probably the lecture was not addressing the exact question. or the question was not formulated in a way to get the proper response.”

explanation: The student notes that questions can be asked during lectures, tutorials, or workshops, indicating the value of accessible opportunities for clarification and feedback within teaching sessions.
quote: “we are allowed to ask any questions, either at the lectures… at the beginning or end, or tutorials, or workshops”

code: Feedback effectiveness shown through later change
explanation: The participant frames good/effective feedback as feedback that leads to observable change in future provision, such as improvements to course selection in the next semester.
quote: “for me that particular feedback, like i'd be able to think, well, this way, next semester, right, when i'm changing courses and stuff, that's when i'd like okay, that worked.”
subtheme: Feedback as a driver of future improvement

explanation: The participant values feedback being acted upon within the semester, particularly around teaching methods and how questions are answered, because this allows students to see results while still enrolled in the course.
quote: “within the semester, like, particularly in terms of maybe the model of teaching or like response to how the questions are being responded to. so if things change within the semester, in regard to the feedback that was given on, this was effective”

explanation: The participant suggests that feedback is effective when students can see tangible results or changes arising from what was said.
quote: “if things change within the semester, in regard to the feedback that was given on, this was effective, so what’s got to see results”

explanation: The student describes frustration that staff acknowledged the feedback process did not make sense but did not provide a clear reason for why it was being done that way, indicating a lack of transparency around feedback practices.
quote: “we know that it doesn't make sense. but we're doing it this way. anyways, because...” and then they didn't like give us a reason why.

explanation: Feedback is framed as something lecturers continue because of institutional bureaucracy rather than because it is meaningful or useful for learning, suggesting students do not see its purpose or impact clearly.
quote: “the lecturers also understand that feedback is kind of a waste of time. but like they sort of have to keep going with it because of the bureaucracy of it all.”

explanation: The student notes that concerns about feedback are commonly discussed among students and tutors, yet staff appeared surprised, suggesting a disconnect between student experiences and institutional awareness. This is relevant to transparency in how feedback issues are recognised and addressed.
quote: “he seemed very surprised for something that is commonly talking about among students and tutors”

explanation: The student describes being told that the lecturer will not provide any more feedback than required, meaning students cannot receive further guidance, apply it, and improve through an ongoing feedback process.
quote: “he just tell us he won't answer. he's not going to give any more feedback that he's already...than he has to”

explanation: The lecturer’s refusal is linked to payment and strike action rather than students’ learning needs, suggesting feedback provision is constrained by institutional circumstances rather than being available to support improvement.
quote: “because the university doesn't pay him anymore. and if we have any problems with this, then we should go on strike”

explanation: Students report being given no meaningful academic course of action to improve their work; the only suggested action is striking, which does not help them act on feedback for learning purposes.
quote: “to find a course of action that you can actually take and not just you know go and strike”

explanation: The exchange highlights students feeling unable to change the feedback situation after being explicitly told no further support will be given.
quote: “you don't have the power to change it… it’s a weird situation to be in a position like this, where you have been explicitly told that ‘i won’t do anything’”
subtheme: Student agency constrained by feedback systems

explanation: The participant describes a lack of transparency in information provided by the university, including not knowing how many students are in a class and being unable to trace or understand the basis of numbers provided. Although this is broader than assignment feedback, it reflects a desire for clearer, more transparent communication from the institution.
quote: "can those data be like will more transparent, because they will tell us like how many people are in this class?... they won't tell us... for all the courses, like everything is so... it's not transparent... they just give you a number. yeah, there's nothing to trace."

explanation: The participant links poor transparency with an impersonal learning experience, suggesting that not knowing basic information about the class reduces their sense of belonging or connection to the course.
quote: "also, like personalization, like, just how impersonal it all feels. in not knowing how many people are on your course, like you don't even know that basically."

explanation: The participant explicitly states that assignment feedback in economics is unhelpful, indicating that the feedback does not provide enough meaningful guidance for learning or improvement.
quote: "the feedback we receive on assignments is so like, unhelpful."

explanation: The participant contrasts the scale and complexity of a substantial project with the very limited feedback received, suggesting the feedback was not detailed enough to understand performance or guide future improvement.
quote: "it was like what seemed like a huge project... like 40 pages... and then we got like eight sentences, of feedback. and that was the most feedback i've ever received for school of econ."

explanation: The participant reports receiving only a sentence per question as feedback, implying that the feedback lacked sufficient explanation, evidence, or clarity to make it useful.
quote: "the most feedback that i received on the course... was like a sentence per question."

explanation: The student describes feedback about course issues being collected or expressed only at the very end, when it can no longer benefit the students who experienced the problem.
quote: "you can only like really realize it's been an issue or say it's been an issue at the end. and then it doesn't help you."
subtheme: Feedback timing must benefit current students

code: No immediate support after identifying course problems
explanation: The student feels that even if the university acknowledges course problems for future cohorts, there is no concrete response to help current students recover from the impact.
quote: "it's not gonna there's no like, 'okay, well, this is what we're going to do to help you now'."
subtheme: Concrete remedial action for current students

code: Feedback lacks opportunity to improve learning before later courses
explanation: The student highlights that unresolved learning gaps continue into later courses, suggesting feedback processes are not part of an ongoing cycle where students can apply improvements before progression.
quote: "it doesn't help the next course builds on what you were supposed to have learned, but you didn't learn."
subtheme: Closing the feedback loop before progression

code: Grade adjustment does not address learning deficits
explanation: The student notes that changing exam grades may respond to poor cohort performance, but it does not help students learn the missing material or prepare for subsequent study.
quote: "they sort of tried to do this a little bit with changing exam grades at the end... but it doesn't help the next course builds on what you were supposed to have learned"
subtheme: Prioritising learning support over grade compensation

explanation: The participant suggests that comparing feedback experiences across courses helps distinguish isolated subject-level issues from broader university-wide problems, implying a need for reliable, consistent approaches across programmes.
quote: it was really nice to kind of hear that in like math and computer science, like some of the same problems are being experienced... it's important to differentiate between kind of like a certain subjects problem and a university wide problem... if it was a university wide problem, they can implement something that everyone has to do

explanation: The participant frames current problems as arising from a changed post-COVID educational context, arguing that previous systems may no longer work. This is relevant background but does not directly specify a quality of good feedback to students.
quote: the system doesn't work anymore because of covid... people are just like, oh, we're going back to normal but normal doesn't exist anymore. like it is the new normal to what we had before
subtheme: Changing educational context and system adaptation

explanation: The participant contrasts problematic feedback experiences with lecturers who listen and change things. This suggests responsiveness to students, but the excerpt concerns staff response to student feedback rather than qualities of feedback given to students.
quote: my lecturers are kind of constantly changing things. like they listen to us really well

explanation: Closed-question surveys can restrict students’ ability to provide detailed, evidence-rich feedback, reducing the usefulness and transparency of the feedback collected.
quote: “only providing closed questions… wouldn't really give my students space to elaborate and actually provide elaborate feedback”

explanation: Students perceived implementation of feedback as inconsistent and fragmented, with limited confidence that feedback leads to concrete change.
quote: “the feedback is difficult to get. it's complicated to get. but the implementation is really scatty. and a lot of people just are quite afraid of actioning feedback.”

explanation: The participant emphasises that feedback is effective when it is read by staff who have the authority to make changes, highlighting the importance of feedback being linked to practical improvement.
quote: "basically whoever has the most influence to change things based on what they've gotten"
subtheme: Reaching those with authority to act

explanation: The participant values weekly class representative forms because they provide a regular mechanism for giving feedback and create at least some expectation that it may be acted upon.
quote: "the main reason why, i guess most of us use that avenue is because it's the most regular, like way we can give feedback and know that there's like, some chance of it being acted upon"

explanation: The participant describes uncertainty about whether feedback reaches the relevant course organiser, suggesting a lack of transparency in the feedback process and uncertainty about how feedback is handled.
quote: "i'm not always sure if it like gets to the right people... sometimes, yeah, it feels like maybe the messages that we send them don't always get to like maybe the course organizer... so, yeah, it feels like there's a kind of disconnect"

code: Different feedback recipients for different issues
explanation: The participant distinguishes between course-specific feedback and wider school-level issues, indicating that effective feedback processes should route information to the appropriate level of responsibility.
quote: "if it's just genuinely to do with that course... all the teaching staff for that course. like if it's more of a general like school issue, then maybe just like the head of the school"
subtheme: Routing feedback to the appropriate level

explanation: The participant suggests that being physically present after lectures enabled more immediate and informal feedback, whereas remote or pandemic conditions required a more formal process. This relates to feedback being easier to provide or receive when it can happen close to the relevant teaching event.
quote: "during, it was definitely a lot harder to give feedback. because you can’t just like go up after a lecture. you had to go through a more formal route."

explanation: The moderator reflects that in-person engagement, being in university buildings, and lecturers recognising students may affect how encouraged students feel to participate in feedback processes. This points to feedback as part of an ongoing relational and engagement cycle rather than a one-off formal act.
quote: "you go to the buildings, you see people in person, lecturers know who you are, possibly, i mean, at least you'll be in the same room as them... do you think there's some kind of difference there in terms of that engagement?"

explanation: The participant states they cannot compare pre- and post-COVID university feedback experiences because they were not at university before COVID. This does not provide substantive thematic material about the qualities of good feedback.
quote: "i'm not really too sure how to answer that question. i wasn't at uni before covid."

explanation: The student describes lunch and class scheduling as preventing attendance at society activities, but this concerns timetable organisation rather than feedback practices.
quote: "we have classes from one to two, but many societies, host all their activities at that time. so we can't attend that activity."

explanation: Students mention the café and teaching building being very busy or small, indicating issues with campus facilities rather than qualities of academic feedback.
quote: "the cafe was extremely busy... and our teaching building is tiny." / "it gets a bit congested."

code: Desire for more convenient lecture location
explanation: The student suggests holding lectures on central campus and practicals at Easter Bush to save time, which relates to logistics and travel rather than feedback.
quote: "why can't we have lectures somewhere in the central campus... and just have our full practicals at easter bush that save us much more time?"

explanation: The participant indicates that feedback collected halfway through a semester may come too late for meaningful changes to be made, suggesting feedback needs to occur earlier while there is still time to act on it.
quote: if you're giving feedback for it halfway through the semester, it's like kind of almost too late to do anything about it. like it might be better to have one like a quarter of the way into semester, like three or four weeks in

explanation: The participant suggests having feedback opportunities both early in the semester and at the end, reflecting a preference for feedback as part of a repeated cycle rather than a single event.
quote: it might be better to have one like a quarter of the way into semester, like three or four weeks in, and then one at the end.

explanation: The participant argues that long surveys discourage responses and that shorter, more frequent surveys may be easier for students to complete, highlighting the need for feedback processes to be manageable and accessible.
quote: having shorter surveys might be a better idea. because having two long surveys instead of say, a short one at the end of every lecture or something like that, meant that people do not want to respond to it.

explanation: The participant is unsure where feelings or feedback would go, speculating that it might be handled by the student association. This relates to uncertainty about feedback mechanisms rather than qualities of good academic feedback to students.
quote: “no, i don't know. because maybe like, student association or something like that.”

explanation: The student indicates uncertainty about where submitted feedback goes and how it is handled after they receive a link, suggesting a lack of transparency in the feedback process.
quote: otherwise, i don't really know how all this information is being processed, we just get sent the link.

explanation: The student suggests that class representatives may be an appropriate channel for class-level feedback because they represent collective student views.
quote: if it's like a class thing, maybe a classrep. that's representing the whole information that i feel... like a course feedback thing

explanation: Receiving a document that lists student questions alongside staff responses is described positively, because it makes the outcome of student feedback visible and understandable.
quote: every time when our class reps have a meeting with the teaching staff or our year administrator, they will send us a document about the question and their response. i think that's quite nice.

explanation: The student notes that response documents are not always provided after routine feedback opportunities, indicating inconsistency in how feedback outcomes are communicated to students.
quote: but i don't think students got that kind of document every time after they have the routine.
subtheme: Consistency in closing the feedback loop

explanation: The student describes receiving an initial acknowledgement that issues are being discussed, but no subsequent update on progress, limiting the usefulness of the feedback cycle.
quote: they say they're trying to figure this out, but i haven't heard back from that. okay, well, how was the process? how is it going on right now?

explanation: The university response is perceived as vague, with students told that discussions are happening but given no clear information about progress or next steps.
quote: it's just like the boss they said, okay, we are discussing this, with a lot of others. okay, and nothing else going on.
subtheme: Clarity about progress and next steps

explanation: The student emphasises that even apparently small issues should be taken seriously rather than brushed off with impractical alternatives.
quote: i know it's like really small matter but, like, don't brush it off. obviously the problem is ‘don't ask us to like oh, well there's another full microwave somewhere else’.

code: Need practical response to student concerns
explanation: The student explains why the microwave issue matters in context, implying that useful feedback responses should address the actual practical constraints students face.
quote: once it's lunchtime in the vet school, it's lunchtime. it's crazy. you can’t find a seat, you have to queue, like, three minutes on a microwave. and then you only have an hour lunch break.

explanation: The participant identifies small, mandatory tutorial groups as a preferable context for giving feedback because students may feel less intimidated and more able to engage with a tutor than with a lecturer. This relates to feedback being accessible and appropriate to the learner’s context.
quote: “in tutorial groups, that would perhaps be the best kind of time and place to give feedback… it’s a small group, so you don’t feel as intimidated… the person who’s like your tutor, is usually not like the lecturer. so it’s also easier to talk to them.”

code: Credit as incentive for giving feedback
explanation: The discussion focuses on incentivising students to provide feedback to the university through course credit, rather than characteristics of good feedback given to students. Therefore, it is not directly relevant to the provided feedback-quality themes.
quote: “i don’t see any issue with even 2-5% of the course credits being given to providing feedback… even 1% i feel would be enough to incentivize students.”

code: Student reps as intermediary for sensitive concerns
explanation: The extract discusses whether student representatives are useful as a midpoint for raising issues when students feel shy or worried about contacting someone directly. This concerns communication channels for raising problems rather than characteristics of effective academic feedback to students.
quote: “if there's an issue. you might feel a bit more shy or a bit more worried that they will share that directly. they might take you the wrong way. so maybe for those cases, i feel the student reps are useful like that midpoint.”

code: Direct contact preferred for simple questions
explanation: One participant indicates that for straightforward questions they prefer to ask directly rather than involve another person. This is about help-seeking or issue escalation rather than feedback quality.
quote: “if i just want questions, i just ask them directly.”

code: Questioning need to involve unrelated staff
explanation: The participant suggests it is unnecessary to message someone they see as irrelevant to the issue, framing it as outside the university’s necessary role. This does not map onto the provided feedback-quality themes.
quote: “i don't think it’s necessary for me to message her and let her, let another irrelevant person know what the issue is… i don’t think it’s like a necessary job for the university.”

explanation: The participant describes sessions as consistently organised but not necessarily interactive or engaging. Although the word 'consistent' is used, this refers to teaching organisation rather than feedback being based on stable criteria, so it is not directly relevant to the feedback themes.
quote: "it's honestly partially out their hands... to make it interactive, just how it's organized, but it's consistent. just that even the ones who are good, they're just good teachers, basically, as opposed to like, engaging"
subtheme: Teaching organisation and engagement rather than feedback

explanation: The participant wants tutors to pass students' concerns to lecturers rather than directing students to approach lecturers themselves. This concerns upward communication from students to staff, not university feedback given to students about their performance.
quote: "they can give our feedback to the lecturers instead of directing us to talk to the lecturers... maybe what the students want, if they can say, ‘okay, i will tell the lectures and see if like anything can be imposed’"

explanation: The moderator summarises the participant's point as tutors helping to facilitate communication between students and lecturers. This is about institutional communication rather than qualities of effective feedback to students.
quote: "if they can facilitate conversation between students and the lectures. yeah."

explanation: Students perceive that representative feedback mechanisms lack value when the university does not act on or implement the feedback they provide.
quote: “if they're not actually making an effort to implement them or figure out a way to get through, then there's no point having student representatives”

code: No clear channel for representative feedback
explanation: The student describes gathering peer feedback but lacking an effective or visible route to pass it on, indicating that the feedback process is not transparent or accessible.
quote: “i've spoken to my classmates about what they feel about the course and things like that. but there's no place to give that feedback.”

explanation: Online feedback requests are described as convenient but easy to ignore or forget, suggesting the method is not well aligned with students’ workload and attention.
quote: “if someone tells me that i need to fill in an online feedback form now, i would probably forget it in another half an hour... i just get swamped with work and then it just doesn't happen.”

explanation: Feedback requested only at the end of a short course is seen as ineffective because there is no opportunity for changes to benefit current students.
quote: “the feedback for that is at the end of the course. so, i don't see the point, because i want you to change something in between the course so that it gets better for the rest of the 2, 3 weeks.”

explanation: A student reports that feedback given by a previous cohort did not lead to changes, undermining the sense that feedback forms part of an improvement cycle.
quote: “she had said that she had given feedback to the course as well... she was like, oh, it’s the same thing. nothing’s changed.”

explanation: The online feedback forms are criticised for being too vague and relying on closed responses, limiting students’ ability to provide meaningful, specific information.
quote: “i personally do not really like how vague they are... there's just like, yes, or no answers, maybe, and that's it.”

explanation: Surveys are perceived as generic and repetitive across subjects, which reduces their relevance to specific learning contexts or course goals.
quote: “they're mostly kind of the same... it doesn't really change, it’s quite the same. it’s like they’ve copy-pasted all the questions”

code: No evidence of action after feedback
explanation: Students do not receive follow-up showing whether feedback has been addressed, making the process feel opaque and ineffective.
quote: “there's no follow up for those things, like, they do not prove or give you any proof of any type of, you know, that they have fixed something... it’s kind of like you're screaming into a void”
subtheme: Visible evidence of response and action

explanation: A student feels institutional surveys are designed around what the university assumes matters, rather than allowing students to identify their actual issues.
quote: “they are not actually... asking the right questions. like, i have a problem. and it's not addressed there. so there's no way that i can actually say that this is a problem to me.”

explanation: The student repeatedly raises lack of support as a student parent, but the issue is neither built into survey questions nor addressed afterwards.
quote: “i always complain about the thing, that i don't have any support because i'm a student parent... and this has never been addressed. and it’s not part of the questions either.”

explanation: The student emphasises that feedback should not be provided so long after the work that they can no longer remember the relevant task or discussion, indicating the importance of receiving feedback while it is still fresh enough to be useful.
quote: “it shouldn’t be so far away that i do not remember my feedback or whatever you need to talk about. so there is a balance there.”
subtheme: Feedback while the task is still memorable

explanation: The extract contains the moderator introducing a question about whether anonymity matters when students give feedback, but there is no substantive student response in the provided text to indicate a view about what makes feedback effective.
quote: “in terms of effective student feedback. do you... is anonymity important for you guys, in terms of giving feedback?”

explanation: The participant describes feedback forms as taking longer than advertised, which reduces willingness to complete them. This relates to feedback processes needing to be manageable and appropriate for the user rather than burdensome.
quote: "sometimes i just decide to skip them, because i know they're going to be too long or something... they always say, like five minutes, it will take you ten. if they said twenty minutes, then it will take you ages"

explanation: The participant often completes feedback while travelling on a phone, but forms are difficult to read or use on a smartphone, causing them to abandon the process. This reflects a need for feedback mechanisms to be accessible and easy to engage with.
quote: "i use my phone to give feedback... there are many times that it’s not really smartphone friendly, the feedback form. so you cannot see it properly on the phone. so it is hard to read and everything. so i just give up many times because of that."

explanation: The participant feels confused about where feedback should be directed, despite the existence of representatives and offices. This indicates a lack of transparency in the feedback system and uncertainty about how feedback is meant to reach the right people.
quote: "i'm always confused. where should i go to when i'm like having any feedback or anything? we do have programme representatives, we do have school representatives... but the whole concept of it doesn't really work."

code: Feedback perceived as not acted upon
explanation: The participant reports that feedback often does not progress or produce visible change, suggesting that feedback is not experienced as part of an effective improvement cycle.
quote: "even if you do give feedback, it doesn't go through most of the of the times. and also even if you say something necessarily it is not being taken care of, or nobody really cares what you're trying to say."

code: Student office redirects rather than resolves issues
explanation: The participant describes being turned away from the student office and told to email, leaving them unsure how to resolve problems. This reflects a lack of clear, accessible feedback handling.
quote: "you go to the student office, they're like, oh, you know, there's really nothing we can do... they're like, ah, you can't come in here. you have to email us."

code: Feedback collection from peers is difficult to facilitate
explanation: A student representative describes the challenge of encouraging classmates to provide feedback without pressuring them. This concerns the usability and accessibility of the feedback process for students.
quote: "it's kind of hard to get everyone to give you feedback, because you like, try not to impose on them being like, okay, you need to tell me what you want right now."

explanation: The participant notes that feedback can be too general or too specific to implement, showing the importance of feedback being concrete enough to act on while still feasible.
quote: "often when you do get something it's really difficult to follow through and like, make it happen, because it's either too general for them to implement, or too specific for them to implement. it's really difficult out there to get that balance."

code: Fear of being too critical when giving feedback
explanation: The student representative worries about presenting feedback without being overly harsh or offending lecturers. This is relevant to clarity and framing, as feedback needs to be communicated in a way that can be understood and received constructively.
quote: "you need to find that balance to tell your professor without being too critical... i'm, like, always kind of trying to figure out if i'm, like, stepping on someone's shoes, or being too harsh towards someone."

code: Lack of concrete meetings with decision-makers
explanation: The participant reports not having formal opportunities to provide feedback to those with authority, limiting whether feedback can lead to change or further discussion.
quote: "i still haven't had any concrete meetings with any sort of authority, i guess, to provide that feedback? i've spoken to my lecturer, but that's about it."

explanation: The participant suggests that lecturers may be willing but unable to act because administrative systems make change difficult. This highlights a breakdown between feedback and practical action.
quote: "she can’t probably get everything done, because it's the administration that is difficult about everything. so yeah, i think it's just like you're in a limbo about how to help."

explanation: The participant suggests that feedback processes are better when students are told what information is being sought and why, rather than being asked to complete a form without context. This relates to making the purpose and expectations of feedback transparent.
quote: “any kind of feedback can be good to just know what is supposed to be better or why they want to hear from us… eusa sent their feedback for you to kind of like give some sort of like, additional information on what, what's going on with that, and why they're asking.”

explanation: The participant contrasts more informative feedback requests with university departments or services that simply send a form without explanation, making the feedback process less clear or accessible to students.
quote: “from the kind of like university departments or services, we usually just get ‘this is a feedback form, just fill it in’, and nothing else.”

explanation: The participant suggests that repeated emails, urgency framing, or voucher incentives are not good motivators for students to provide feedback. This concerns encouraging students to give feedback rather than qualities of feedback given to students, so it does not align with the specified feedback-quality themes.
quote: "i don't think it's a good factor with like, just keep on sending emails or make it an urgent, email, or even like these voucher things like you can get, you'll get this in order to get feedback."
subtheme: Ineffective feedback solicitation and engagement tactics

explanation: The participant describes feedback as informal suggestions from society members about desired events and speakers, rather than as formal feedback. This indicates a participatory feedback process where input can shape future activity.
quote: “we always are for women in politics are asking the members like, ‘what do you guys want to see? what kind of events? who do you want to speak?’ that kind of stuff. and people give suggestions.”

explanation: The participant explicitly distinguishes this kind of input from formal feedback, suggesting that some feedback processes may not be recognised as feedback when they occur informally.
quote: “i guess i don't really think about it as like a formal feedback.”

explanation: The participant contrasts lectures with societies, suggesting that the absence of a strong lecturer-student hierarchy makes it easier for members to contribute to shaping activities. This is relevant to feedback culture, but does not map directly onto the specified feedback-quality themes.
quote: “in a lecture setting, there's like that difference between lecturer and students... but in a society there’s not that kind of barier... if you're a member of society, you also participate in contributing to what the society is actually about.”

explanation: The participant suggests that combining in-class and email-based approaches is useful because it allows students to engage with feedback processes whether or not they attend class. This relates to making feedback communication accessible and manageable for learners.
quote: "i think both is kind of a good solution. because if you're doing it in class, it's much easier to just fill out a single card, like while you're already there. and then like, obviously, if you're not in class, for whatever reason, then having emails."

code: In-class feedback is easier to complete
explanation: Completing feedback during class is described as convenient because students are already present and can respond immediately, reducing the effort required to engage.
quote: "if you're doing it in class, it's much easier to just fill out a single card, like while you're already there."

explanation: Automated emails and large numbers of announcements make feedback-related communication easy to miss or ignore. This suggests that feedback delivery can become ineffective when communication is excessive or not prioritised clearly.
quote: "we have automated emails too. but it's to the point where they're so flooded that people don't check them a lot. because professors release, like, 20 announcements at the same time or something like that."

explanation: University staff identified that the student was struggling during a practical and initiated contact, suggesting feedback/support was prompted by observed performance rather than waiting for the student to ask.
quote: “in that practical, a few weeks ago, just they find me not doing the things so well as other students, and they just asked my name. and another staff sent me an email and she said, as a student support session”

explanation: The student describes being reluctant to ask for help because they feared being judged. This is relevant contextual information about barriers to engaging with feedback/support, but it does not directly fit the provided feedback-quality themes.
quote: “at the very beginning of starting here, i was too scared of asking for help, because i'm still afraid of getting of being judged.”

explanation: The participant describes attempting to raise a concern through university contacts but receiving a response that felt dismissive rather than constructive or helpful. This does not directly describe qualities of academic feedback, so it is coded as not thematically relevant to the provided feedback themes.
quote: "it was kind of like a i'm sorry, that's not possible" ... "yeah, pretty much" [in response to being asked if they were brushed off]

explanation: The participant describes a mid-term feedback form being administered directly during a tutorial to ensure the tutor received student feedback. This concerns students giving feedback to the university rather than the university providing feedback to students, so it is not directly relevant to the provided feedback-quality themes.
quote: “there was a mid-term feedback form. and then the tutor gave us directly in the tutorial to make sure they received some feedback.”

explanation: The participant contrasts in-class feedback collection with feedback forms sent by email, which they believe are commonly ignored. This relates to feedback collection mechanisms rather than qualities of effective feedback to students.
quote: “there are also some, like feedback forms that are sent via email. but those i think is for.... people ignored.”
subtheme: Low engagement with remote feedback channels

code: Perceived course value but poor learning experience
explanation: The participant distinguishes between recognising the course as useful/essential and experiencing its delivery and assessment as ineffective. This is relevant context, but it does not directly describe feedback characteristics.
quote: everyone is very clear that it's useful... for psychology, we need to know, obviously, these things. it's just the way that they do it somehow just makes so many people hate it... the assessments are super difficult, and the marks are really low.

explanation: The speaker notes that some prior feedback appears to have been incorporated into the course, particularly through improvements to labs, weekly questions, and exercises. This reflects feedback as part of an iterative improvement cycle.
quote: i think they have implemented some of the feedback... i have seen some changes with past years... during our labs, i find that the labs are a bit better than they used to be, the questions that we have to answer every week. and the exercises that we have to do.

explanation: The participant recognises that feedback may be acted on, but describes the process as slow, reducing its usefulness for current students. This relates to the importance of feedback being timely enough to have impact.
quote: i think they have implemented some of the feedback. it may be quite slow because it's the first year that they're doing this.

code: Difficulty catching up after poor initial delivery
explanation: The speaker suggests that because the course started poorly during COVID, later feedback and changes struggle to remedy the learning experience. This reflects delayed or retrospective feedback having reduced impact once students have already fallen behind.
quote: it started out badly with covid. because everything's online. and now it's really hard to catch up and make it the best, even with like feedback and stuff.

explanation: The participant reports that the course receives substantial feedback but that only some issues are addressed. This undermines the feedback loop because students do not see consistent opportunities for their feedback to lead to improvement.
quote: ours is a really, really good example of a course that receives huge amounts of feedback, mostly negative, but they are very, very selective in what they actually choose to change.

explanation: A persistent complaint about the course credit weighting is described as repeatedly raised by students but consistently ignored. This highlights a failure to use recurring feedback to make meaningful adjustments.
quote: there's been a consistent complaint, for example, that it's a 10-credit course... they said, oh, yeah, we hear it every single time... that's feedback that has consistently, repeatedly... been an issue, that they have very, very consistently chosen to ignore.

explanation: The department’s numerical justification for the course workload is perceived as not matching students’ lived experience. This relates to feedback and course expectations needing to be transparent and grounded in observable evidence.
quote: they justify it by, this is how much time we expect you to work on it... it should equate to all the other reading courses. the reality is that it isn't actually true, in practice. so whilst they can justify it with some nice set of numbers, it doesn't match.

code: Gradual course redesign in response to feedback
explanation: The participant acknowledges that the department has made structural changes to introduce the material more gradually, suggesting that some feedback has been converted into concrete course adjustments.
quote: they have chosen to try and alter the course and how it used to only be over two years, now it’s over three years, so they've tried to sort of make the introduction a little bit more gradual.

code: Lack of transparency about course content before enrolment
explanation: The speaker argues that students are not clearly informed in advance about the heavy statistics and coding component. This reflects a lack of transparent information about expectations and goals before students begin the course.
quote: it's not advertised as such a huge component in the course... i had no information that such a significant amount of the course was... intense statistics and data coding... students should know what they're coming in for.

code: Need to consider repeated feedback even when difficult
explanation: The participant explicitly states that recurring student feedback should be taken seriously even when it is inconvenient. This captures the importance of a reliable feedback cycle in which student input is recognised and used for adjustment.
quote: feedback repeated again and again and again, should be considered even if you don't like it, such as, it being only 10 credits, as much as it's complicated in the way it's designed.

explanation: The excerpt contains only procedural interview setup and the participant introducing their course/year, with no substantive discussion of feedback practices or qualities of good feedback.
quote: “yeah, my name is s1, and i study history of art in year two.”

explanation: The moderator discusses the timing, group/session identifier, and whether the participant brought an image; this is contextual administration rather than thematically relevant content about feedback.
quote: “so the time is 1408. and it's the group 8 eca. so you can introduce yourself now if you'd like.”

code: Mode affects willingness to give feedback
explanation: The participant contrasts online/electronic and face-to-face methods, suggesting they may be less likely to provide feedback when asked online and more inclined to raise concerns face-to-face. This concerns barriers to students giving feedback rather than what makes feedback to students effective, so it is not aligned with the specified feedback-quality themes.
quote: “i will compare like electronic and physical. whereas i feel like if the lecture is just asked online, not do it... perhaps not face to face, i wouldn't actually do it if i had more concerns.”

code: Missed opportunity to give positive feedback
explanation: The participant notes that not providing feedback prevents them from telling lecturers what they are doing well. This relates to student-to-staff feedback opportunities rather than university feedback to students, so it falls outside the provided thematic categories.
quote: “and that's bad, because i don't get to like, tell them what they're good at. which is something that you might not know.”

explanation: The participant suggests that class representatives should be introduced clearly at the start of semester so students know who they are. This concerns awareness of representation/communication channels rather than the quality or characteristics of academic feedback to students.
quote: "introduce the class reps at the beginning of the semester, like in person, in front of everyone in the lecture theatre... that kind of made me know the names of our class reps"

explanation: The discussion notes that introducing representatives is harder for later-year students because they may not share one large class setting. This is about logistical communication with students, not directly about feedback being goal-referenced, actionable, timely, or otherwise pedagogically effective.
quote: "for third and fourth years, it's hard because there isn't one big class for them to introduce themselves in"

explanation: The participant expresses a desire for university communication or engagement to focus more on campus culture and feeling connected to the institution, but this does not directly relate to feedback on student performance or learning.
quote: "it's more needs to be on campus culture, i guess, especially if we're always going out. i i want to feel connected to the school."

explanation: The participant discusses whether they would attach their name when giving feedback to the university, noting that this depends on personality and how strongly they feel. This concerns students providing feedback to the institution rather than qualities of academic feedback given to students.
quote: "to certain things, i think it’s very personality wise, if i feel very strongly about something, i'll just say my name. like i have something to say about this or like sometimes people are just like, here's an issue"

explanation: The student describes course feedback being collected too late for any changes to be made while their cohort is still experiencing the course, reducing its usefulness.
quote: it often felt like it was asked too late for the feedback to be implemented with, like, to request feedback.
subtheme: Feedback collected early enough to act

explanation: The student feels feedback is framed as useful only for the next cohort, leaving their own cohort without an opportunity to benefit from or act upon the feedback cycle.
quote: so where it was, like, ‘for the next cohort’ like, okay, what about my cohort?
subtheme: Closing the feedback loop for current students

explanation: The student refers generally to staff saying things students are unhappy with, but the extract does not provide enough detail to link this clearly to a specific feature of effective feedback.
quote: they're usually saying something that the students are not happy with.

explanation: The participant highlights uncertainty about whether feedback leads to change, suggesting that a good feedback process should make outcomes or implementation visible to those providing it.
quote: “how do we know that feedback is, like, implemented into something?”

code: Ease and efficiency of feedback process
explanation: The participant perceives the university as trying to make feedback easy, but notes that giving and requesting feedback can still be difficult, pointing to the need for a user-friendly and efficient process.
quote: “i think they want to make it as easy a process as possible. but, in general, just giving feedback and asking for feedback is something that's quite hard… how to make the whole process as efficient as possible.”

explanation: The participant describes repeated requests for feedback across courses; this concerns institutional solicitation of feedback rather than feedback given to students, so it is only indirectly relevant to the study aim.
quote: “i always feel like i'm getting requests for feedback. in every single one of my courses, it's kind of like the university is begging for… feedback”

explanation: The participant suggests that collecting feedback from students in person may be more useful and engaging than relying on forms. However, this refers to students giving feedback to the university rather than university feedback to students, so it is not directly thematically relevant to the provided feedback-to-learners themes.
quote: “i feel like maybe collecting feedback from people in person might be more useful... i'm probably in the minority for filling them out often... i think it might work better.”

code: Delayed fee status decision blocks action
explanation: The student describes a delayed response about fee status, which had practical consequences because they could not proceed with enrolment-linked housing applications. This highlights the importance of feedback being prompt while students can still act on it.
quote: "it took like weeks for them to get back to me... because of the student fee status that wouldn't be confirmed, i couldn't apply for housing. and if i would have applied for the housing a week or two later, i would have never gotten a house"

explanation: The student had to research government rules themselves and use these to challenge the University's decision, suggesting the University's communication about fee status was unclear and not transparently grounded in accessible evidence or criteria.
quote: "the university said, no, you have to pay the international fees... i read through the government page, and i said, oh, by the way, government says this, this, this, so you kind of have to because the government says this"

explanation: A promised update or escalation was not completed until the student chased it, showing a breakdown in the ongoing feedback loop where information should be followed up and acted upon consistently over time.
quote: "they're finally like, oh, well, we'll let them know... after like a week, i was like, hey, so have you heard anything, what's the update? silence for five days, then they're like... no, i haven't quite done that yet"

explanation: Students indicate they do not know where to direct complaints or feedback about University services, suggesting a lack of clear, accessible communication channels.
quote: "we don't know where to give feedback, because we're actually giving feedback to you right now... if you have a complaint about the finance team because of all of these, where do you go?"

code: Students need actionable points of contact
explanation: The students' uncertainty about who to speak to and whether they should contact managers themselves indicates that University communication did not provide concrete next steps or clear routes for resolving problems.
quote: "can you please tell somebody? can you please tell somebody? like, is there anybody i can speak to?"

explanation: The moderator summarises students’ preference for being told specific points about what has been heard from them and what has changed, rather than receiving vague assurances. This reflects feedback being clear, observable, and transparent about its impact.
quote: so definitely a lot of mentions of actually hearing back and hearing what has changed. and so do you think all of you would say that when you get specific points put down for what they're hearing from you that that makes much more of a difference than simply hearing that things may have changed the next time?

explanation: Students report that lecturers/tutors do not make it explicit that they welcome feedback, leaving students unsure whether they are permitted or expected to offer it. This concerns feedback culture rather than the quality of feedback given to students, so it is not directly aligned with the provided feedback-quality themes.
quote: "the tutors or lecturers don't really ever make clear that they want feedback... i never really felt that i was in a position to give them feedback. so i never did."
subtheme: Permission and psychological safety to give feedback

code: Repeated feedback requests perceived as excessive
explanation: One student describes lecturers repeatedly asking for feedback across consecutive lectures. Although initial requests and apparent responsiveness were valued, repeated requests without clear visible change were perceived as overkill.
quote: "two of my courses have actually asked in the lectures for feedback... that's really helpful... they're like, ‘oh, okay, we'll change that and stuff’. but then when they do it the next lecture as well... what has changed that more people would give feedback like this a bit overkill."

code: Need to show changes after feedback
explanation: The student questions what has changed between repeated feedback requests, implying that feedback processes are more meaningful when learners can see that prior feedback has led to action or adjustment.
quote: "but then when they do it the next lecture as well as like, what, like a week later, what has changed that more people would give feedback"

code: Fear of unsolicited feedback seeming confrontational
explanation: Students feel uncomfortable approaching staff with feedback when it has not been requested, worrying that it may be interpreted as criticism or an attack rather than constructive input. This is about interpersonal dynamics around giving staff feedback, not directly about feedback to students.
quote: "i’d feel weird, just sort of like going up to a lecturer or tutor or something going, ‘hey, i don't like what you said that blah, blah, blah’... it feels sort of like an attack... especially when they’re not asking for it."
subtheme: Permission and psychological safety to give feedback

explanation: Students want the University to explicitly acknowledge that feedback has been received and show how it will respond, rather than leaving students unsure whether their feedback was noticed.
quote: "there should be an obligation to acknowledge feedback to the students, and to demonstrate what kind of like plan... what... actions they think should be taken"

explanation: Students value feedback processes that include later follow-up, so they can see whether changes have actually been made after their feedback.
quote: "then have an overview of like, down the line to check with us like two weeks later to show what changes have been made"

explanation: The suggested two-week follow-up indicates that feedback should be responded to within a practical timeframe while the issue is still current and meaningful to students.
quote: "check with us like two weeks later to show what changes have been made"
subtheme: Prompt follow-up while issues are current

explanation: Students want responses to feedback to address specific issues directly, rather than giving vague or generic replies that do not lead to meaningful change.
quote: "it would be very helpful if there are like very specific questions in response... like, didn't you do this exact thing we didn't like"

explanation: The participant criticises responses that appear to acknowledge feedback but are too vague to produce actual improvements, highlighting the need for concrete and visible action.
quote: "so like, they see that they actually does not say something very... that doesn't actually change anything, like actual specific stuff"

explanation: Students want the University to summarise what it has heard from the majority and clearly state the steps it will take as a result, making the feedback process concrete and usable.
quote: "we've seen that the majority of you have said this. and so from this, these are the steps that we're going to take"
subtheme: Clear next steps from student input

explanation: Students describe a cycle where the University implements changes and then returns to students to ask whether the changes are working, reflecting ongoing refinement.
quote: "like two weeks, go back to students and be like, okay, so continue to implement it. isn't like better, like isn't working"

explanation: The moderator summarises students’ concern that existing feedback mechanisms may be acceptable, but the feedback is ineffective because staff do not acknowledge or implement it. This relates to feedback needing to be part of a cycle where information is acted on rather than ignored.
quote: “the emails that you get, and the surveys that you fill out, and the methods of feedback are fine. but it's the fact that they're not being put into practice.”

explanation: Students describe a lecturer justifying limited support by blaming students for not attending lectures, which made students feel their effort was not recognised. This is relevant to the perceived usefulness and responsiveness of feedback/support processes, though it is only indirectly about feedback to students.
quote: “she used the fact that some students didn't go to the lecture… that's why they said it's not our problem is the students problem. makes us very uncomfortable, because some students put the effort.”

explanation: A student argues that recorded lectures mean non-attendance does not necessarily indicate lack of effort, because students may engage in different ways. This concerns staff assumptions about student behaviour rather than a clear feature of good feedback.
quote: “if the student doesn’t attend that lecture, they could watch the lecture online. so it's not as though students aren't putting in the effort. they're just putting it in different ways.”

code: Lack of financial support for international students
explanation: The participant describes the university as not providing adequate financial assistance or flexible payment options for international students facing high accommodation costs. This concerns student financial support rather than feedback on academic performance.
quote: "they do not really provide that kind of financial support... i tried to ask for some type of, maybe a payment plan... because you can't get an accommodation loan from the government if you are an international student... they don't provide any help."
subtheme: Financial support gaps for international students

code: Support processes perceived as inaccessible or impractical
explanation: The participant criticises the financial support portal as closed, narrowly applicable, and slow to process, making it ineffective for urgent need. This is about administrative support rather than feedback quality.
quote: "the portal closed on october 5. babe, it's november. second of all, it only applies to very specific things. and then it also takes them three weeks to process."
subtheme: Barriers to accessing timely institutional support

code: Funding allocation perceived as unfairly targeted
explanation: The participant argues that university funding appears directed toward particular demographic groups rather than those with the greatest financial need. This concerns bursary allocation and institutional equity, not student feedback.
quote: "a lot of the funding that the university offers is for chinese students... there's a lot of people who really desperately need it... and they don't get anything."

code: Need-based support should reflect individual circumstances
explanation: The participant suggests the university should consider students' specific financial situations rather than broad categories such as international status or parental income. Although this relates to personalisation of support, it does not address feedback on learning.
quote: "they're not really looking at like, your specific thing. they're like, oh, you're an international student... i'm not one of the people that like, comes here to ball out."
subtheme: Need for individualised assessment of student circumstances

explanation: The participant describes severe stress caused by unstable accommodation and financial strain, including uncertainty about where they will sleep. This is relevant to student welfare but not to feedback practices.
quote: "there's been too many times where i've had to sit in my bed the night before worrying about where i'm going to sleep the next day... i have all of my stuff on the road on the street."
subtheme: Impact of financial hardship on wellbeing and housing security

explanation: The participant ends by expressing a need for community in response to financial and housing insecurity. This concerns belonging and institutional care rather than academic feedback.
quote: "i don't know, we need to have some sort of community."
subtheme: Need for community and belonging during hardship

explanation: The student indicates that being asked to judge how well they are doing before any submitted work has been assessed is unhelpful because they lack evidence of their performance. This highlights the need for feedback questions to be timed around meaningful opportunities to evaluate progress.
quote: “there's that one question ‘can you assess like how well you think you're doing’ but for a number of my courses. i haven't submitted anything yet. it's all like riding on the final exam or the final paper and so i'm like, i don't know.”
subtheme: Feedback timed to meaningful assessment points

explanation: The student suggests that without submitted assessments or interim indicators, they cannot compare their current performance against course expectations. Feedback processes need clear goals or criteria so students can understand where they stand.
quote: “it's not about how we we think we're doing, it's about what the course are.”
subtheme: Clear performance criteria and reference points

explanation: Students describe feedback forms as almost identical across schools and courses, with only names changed. This suggests that feedback collection is not sufficiently tailored to observable features of each course, making it less transparent and meaningful.
quote: “every school has almost the same feedback form… the only thing that changes is the name of the lectures and tutors, and nothing else.”

explanation: The student questions whether written feedback is actually read or whether responses are simply counted. This reflects a lack of transparency about how feedback is processed and whether students’ comments have any visible impact.
quote: “are they given a kind of like reading through it? or do they have like a some sort of stuff where you just kind of count the the points that we make?”
subtheme: Transparency about how feedback is used

explanation: The reliance on satisfaction scales is presented as limiting because it allows feedback to be processed without engaging with students’ more detailed experiences. This suggests feedback needs to provide concrete information rather than broad evaluative ratings alone.
quote: “most of it is still like, ‘satisfied? very satisfied, very dissatisfied’. so, you know, technically, you don't even have to read that.”

explanation: Students report receiving multiple identical forms in succession, making the process disengaging. This implies that feedback mechanisms should be designed in a user-friendly way that does not overwhelm participants with repetitive requests.
quote: “they send the forms out… in succession… course one, course two, course three, and it's all the same form… i guess i don't do all these forms like, one go.”

explanation: The student suggests distributing feedback tasks across students rather than asking each student to complete several similar forms. This reflects the view that reducing burden would make feedback more engaging and improve its quality.
quote: “instead of like one student having to fill out all three courses, they will need like fill up one course, i think that will be much more interesting. and that will be definitely up the quality of feedback.”

explanation: The repeated use of the same form across courses leads the student to question whether the feedback is relevant. Effective feedback mechanisms should capture course-specific evidence that can be understood and acted upon.
quote: “it's the same thing. exactly, it's only the course name changes, like, is this even going to be relevant?”

explanation: The participant suggests paper surveys are a more practical and effective method for students to provide feedback to the university, as they are easier to complete and return than attending in-person sessions.
quote: “i don't mind doing surveys… they’re probably the most appropriate or even like paper surveys… they're more willing to do it if it's a paper form. cause then they’ve got to give it back.”

explanation: The participant identifies in-person feedback sessions as time-consuming and difficult for commuting students due to travel and access issues.
quote: “having an in person one again, that's also time consuming. and then it's hard to get to the building sometimes, especially when you commute.”
subtheme: Barriers to participation in feedback processes

explanation: The participant explains that online surveys can be missed because they get lost among university emails, making them less effective as a feedback collection method.
quote: “online? yeah. because sometimes you just get lost with all your emails, you've just missed the survey. if there were physical paper forms - better.”

code: Fear of negative consequences when giving feedback
explanation: The participant describes a barrier to providing feedback when they expect the recipient may respond badly, leading them to consider how to protect themselves from adverse effects. This concerns interpersonal risk in giving feedback rather than qualities of good feedback from the University to students, so it is not directly aligned with the specified feedback-quality themes.
quote: “sometimes when i feel like the person i want to give the feedback to will not take kindly to it, then i do have a barrier, kind of like how to do it to also shield myself from, like, adverse effect.”
subtheme: Emotional risk and vulnerability in giving feedback

explanation: The participant notes that giving feedback to a tutor or professor about comments that felt uncomfortable or targeting places students in a vulnerable position. This reflects emotional risk and power dynamics in student-to-staff feedback, rather than criteria for effective feedback given to students.
quote: “if you feel like something that the tutor or the professor said that made you uncomfortable or that felt targeting to you, i think that's like puts you in a really vulnerable position to that, give them feedback about that.”

explanation: The participant highlights that providing feedback may require disclosing membership of a group or an invisible condition, which can make the student feel exposed. quote: "she very consistently was like asking for feedback, even just like one on one feedback, or up until the very end, she was like, send me feedback"

code: Reassurance that feedback will be acted on
