explanation: The participant notes that students who engage in feedback processes are likely those already motivated to do so, while others may not respond. This relates to students giving feedback to the institution, not characteristics of good feedback given to students.
quote: "we are here because we volunteered. and we're the sort of people who want to give feedback. i think that's like a self-selection process. there are definitely people in the program who probably never responded to surveys"
subtheme: Barriers and biases in student voice participation

code: Valuing opportunities to give institutional feedback
explanation: The participant positively contrasts their current university experience, where there are opportunities to provide feedback, with a prior context where such opportunities were absent or unclear. This is about institutional mechanisms for student voice rather than feedback to students on learning.
quote: "in my school in the us, like, we never really had opportunities to give a lot of feedback. or maybe they did, and i just didn't know. but yeah, so i think this is quite good."
subtheme: Value of accessible institutional feedback channels

explanation: The participant speculates that university or school financial priorities may shape what staff can do, but this does not directly address the qualities of effective feedback to students.
quote: "the school or the uni wants to make money and the teachers are like ‘oh you can’t do this’... and we’re like ‘it sucks’... literally who knows? it's like, completely okay, beyond our programme."

explanation: The participant describes receiving guidance that influenced their UCAS application and understanding of available class options. This relates to university advice rather than feedback on performance, so it is not thematically relevant to the feedback themes.
quote: “i applied for history of art, because when i spoke to someone, they said that i could pick businesses one of my other classes.”

explanation: The student describes a lecturer responding defensively and rebutting concerns raised through the SSLC, suggesting that feedback is not being taken on board or used as part of an improvement cycle.
quote: the students rep, they tried to, like, tell me about the problems. and then she was quite aggressive... kind of, like, rebut all the arguments

explanation: Students were seeking solutions to identified problems, but the response they received did not provide usable guidance or a constructive path forward.
quote: because the students were just looking for solutions for those questions. and then she said, like, it's illegal to give answers.

explanation: The moderator explicitly frames the issue as students potentially feeling that their feedback is not valued, which may reduce motivation to provide feedback in future.
quote: do you think like that makes students feel that the feedback isn't valued in general? what's the incentive to provide it in the first place?

explanation: The participant suggests that feedback may be improved when provided by someone without a personal investment, implying a need for greater objectivity and reduced bias in assessment or feedback processes.
quote: "make someone who doesn't have a personal investment or resource get more objective about it."

code: No visible response to student feedback
explanation: The participant describes being asked for feedback by a programme representative but perceiving that nothing happened afterwards, highlighting the importance of feedback being part of a visible cycle where information leads to response or adjustment.
quote: “our program rep asked us for some feedback. and then nothing of it.”

explanation: The participant suggests that even when feedback forms are completed, any resulting change may occur years later, reducing the usefulness of the feedback because it is not timely enough to benefit the students who provided it.
quote: “even if i provide the feedback, the feedback will be like, the change will be made, like after like, two years, three years”

code: Feedback forms ask for improvement suggestions
explanation: The participant notes that course feedback forms ask how content can be improved, indicating a mechanism intended to gather concrete information for future improvement, although the effectiveness is limited by delayed action.
quote: “it’s just basically asking, asking, like, how can we improve on like, the content or, like rate us on a scale of like five stars”

explanation: Participants describe feedback forms being distributed at different points in the course, including mid-term and toward the end, which relates to whether feedback is collected early enough for action to be taken while it can still affect the learning experience.
quote: “some do it like in the middle and some towards the end” / “probably like mid term, or like after the finals, or before the finals”

code: Survey feedback should inform course improvement
explanation: The participant states that survey feedback should be read by relevant staff so that it can be used to improve the course. This concerns feedback being acted upon, but it is about student evaluations of the course rather than feedback given to students.
quote: “everything they have to read the results in order for them to make an improvement of the course. so yes, they do have to read the feedback.”

explanation: The participant explains their reason for attending the session was to share their opinion and receive the voucher, rather than describing characteristics of effective feedback.
quote: “i wanted to get involved in these feedback sessions. i did want to give my opinion. and also because of the voucher. that did motivate me”

explanation: The extract provides demographic and course context for the participants but does not include views or experiences about what makes feedback effective.
quote: “i'm a second year postgraduate student… it's in psychology… psychological research methods, masters.” / “i'm doing my second year in cognitive science… my department is ppls.”

explanation: The moderator introduces the feedback-related drawing task, but no participant response about feedback is provided in this extract.
quote: “we asked you to bring a sketch, or a drawing with you about how you feel about feedback. so do you want to go first and share your drawing?”

explanation: The student values feedback/response that acknowledges their concern and explains the rationale behind course decisions, making the institution's position clearer and more transparent.
quote: "all i really want is like an explanation as to if i say like, oh, i don't like the way this course is structured because of xyz. and they go okay, i hear you, but this is like, why it's done like that. i feel like that's way more effective than just like, not responding at all"

explanation: The student frames effective feedback as involving acknowledgement and listening, even when the issue is not directly solved. This reflects the importance of clear, accessible communication that makes the student feel their input has been received.
quote: "90% of the time when people complain they don't actually want their problems solved, they just want to be listened to. and i think honestly, like, that's how i feel about feedback."

explanation: The student identifies office hours or appointments with course staff as useful mechanisms for raising problems and receiving responses, suggesting feedback is more effective when there is an available channel for ongoing discussion.
quote: "it would be nice to have some sort of opportunity to come to the course organiser, or course secretary and talk to them... ‘if anyone has any problems, they can just come to the office hours or schedule an appointment’. and that's really working, but not every course does."

explanation: The student notes that some courses provide clear opportunities to discuss problems while others do not, indicating inconsistency in how feedback channels are provided across the university experience.
quote: "that's really working, but not every course does."

explanation: The participant does not provide a substantive view on what makes feedback effective, but asks the moderator to clarify the question with an example.
quote: g1s1 09:18: "could you give me an example?"

explanation: The discussion raises the issue that some student voices may be over- or under-represented in feedback mechanisms, such as lecture-based paper forms only reaching students who attend and may already be more satisfied. This concerns institutional feedback collection rather than feedback given to students, so it does not fit the provided feedback-quality themes.
quote: moderator 2 09:21: "the people who come to lectures actually quite enjoyed the lecture... but the people who don't come to lecture, they don't like the lecture and there was no way they're gonna be encouraged to give feedback... they might be under represented in some way."

code: University choice based on business possibility
explanation: The participant identifies the possibility of doing business as the main reason for choosing the university, but this does not provide substantive information about what makes feedback good or effective.
quote: “did you think it affected like, the possibility of doing business was a factor you coming here in the first place?” / “yeah, that was pretty much. that was the reason i chose this university.”

explanation: Semester course feedback is used to adjust teaching for future students, but this suggests feedback may arrive too late for the students who provided it to benefit directly.
quote: we do course feedback every semester, regarding how we feel about the course. and then all teaching staff will change accordingly to current students feedback for next years students.

explanation: Midterm feedback is valued because staff can hear students’ views and adjust teaching while the current cohort can still benefit.
quote: we have the midterm feedback, you just allow the staff to hear what we are thinking and adjust the way of teaching so our current student will still benefit from the last half of the teaching. i think that is good.

explanation: Students describe an ongoing system in which feedback is gathered and teaching is changed, indicating a feedback cycle across semesters and cohorts.
quote: that's kind of like an integrated system for all the juniors, which i think is fine.

explanation: The student feels staff shift between options in response to different student preferences, making it difficult to establish a stable approach to teaching design.
quote: it's really hard to find a good balance, because teaching staff just bounce from a to b, b, back to a to b, because that's what students want

code: Practical timing changed but balance unclear
explanation: Feedback about insufficient practical time led to adding time, but the change then became too long, showing difficulty turning feedback into proportionate, effective action.
quote: last year, students like you don't have enough time for practical. and so they gave us like an extra hour... this is just way too long... it's gonna go back to now, which is like really hard to find the balance

code: Different student needs create feedback conflict
explanation: Students’ feedback differs over whether exotic animal clinical skills should be compulsory or optional, highlighting the need for clear shared criteria when acting on feedback.
quote: students suggested that they should have exotics animal clinical skills practical but some students think that that should be optional because not every student are interested in that topic

explanation: Students report that transport issues are discussed in town halls but feel there is no meaningful action, so their feedback does not seem to lead to practical improvement.
quote: we have had a lot of townhall meetings addressing this issue that's affecting students every day for missing classes and being late... we can't do anything about it. and we just feel like the students are not being heard.

code: Feedback linked to immediate attendance consequences
explanation: The bus issue is significant because it affects compulsory practical attendance, showing students need institutional responses while there is still opportunity to prevent academic disruption.
quote: it's compulsory. 100% attendance for all our practical - like imagine just losing one and then if you can't fit another replacement on to your schedule and just quite a big trouble and hassle.

explanation: Students perceive that the university often collects their feedback but does not report back on what was said or what will change, limiting the sense of an ongoing improvement cycle.
quote: i don’t think they will give us feedback on our feedback. they just take our feedback, and probably just take it, yeah.

explanation: The participant suggests that when staff share what feedback was received and how they will respond, it makes the process clearer and reassures students that their input has a purpose.
quote: in a lot of cases, when they gather feedback, they're not like, oh, this is what people said. so we're going to try and do that. which i think, it would be helpful to know that we are being listened to and that when we're filling stuff, it's for a reason.

code: Acting on class feedback during teaching
explanation: A positive example is given where student feedback about topics to revisit was translated into a concrete teaching action in a later lecture.
quote: they were like, oh, most people voted for this. so we're gonna go over this again.

explanation: The feedback was gathered about what students wanted to cover in the remaining weeks, making it useful because there was still time for staff to respond within the course.
quote: it was more the specifics that you like, that we all wanted to go into for the last remaining weeks, like it was anything we want to cover again, that kind of thing.

explanation: The participant describes uncertainty about how to contact the university as a whole, indicating a concern about communication pathways rather than the quality or characteristics of academic feedback to students.
quote: i don't even know how i would contact the uni as a whole. i only contacted the course.

explanation: The excerpt only establishes that a student submitted a drawing and is being asked to explain it; it does not contain substantive discussion about feedback qualities or processes.
quote:
primary moderator  01:28
so i've received some drawings from i guess this was from s4.

s4  01:36
y yeah. 

primary moderator  01:36
yeah. so this was her drawing. so do you want to explain it?

explanation: The discussion suggests that the feedback or institutional response may not provide anything that can be acted on or changed, limiting its usefulness for improvement.
quote: "there's nothing they can do about it sort of thing"

explanation: The participant describes broad feedback requests across multiple courses as harder to answer because they require tracking down different memories, implying that feedback is more useful when linked to a specific focus or context.
quote: "it's just, i guess, a bit harder to track down. or when you think about, like when you have to think about different courses. it makes it a bit harder, i guess, than if they're just asking about one specific topic."

explanation: The participant recognises value in asking about a general issue, but suggests that if something is wrong, the feedback should allow specification for the relevant course. This indicates a need for feedback to be clear and connected to observable contexts.
quote: "it's sometimes better, like in that case, to ask about a general thing. and then maybe if something's wrong, you could just specify that for that course."

explanation: Surveys conducted during class are described as less time consuming because students do not need to separately track down memories later. This suggests feedback processes are more accessible when embedded in a convenient setting.
quote: "a lot of surveys are conducted during the classes... the professor just asks you to fill in this form... so i think it's less time consuming"

explanation: The participant notes that completing feedback in class reduces the need to recall specific memories afterwards, suggesting that feedback is easier and potentially more accurate when gathered close to the learning experience.
quote: "it's less time consuming if you do need to track down the specific memories about something."
subtheme: Capturing feedback close to the learning experience

explanation: The availability of a text entry box is valued because it allows students to point out particular concerns rather than only selecting ratings, making the feedback more specific and informative.
quote: "if you have something to point out, you can just add it in the... there's like a text entry. you can just say it there."

explanation: The participant distinguishes between simply rating items and giving useful constructive suggestions, implying that numerical or star ratings alone may not provide enough information for improvement.
quote: "i haven't given like, that useful, like, constructive suggestions. i just like to like rate stuff, you know. just give the stars."

explanation: For urgent problems, the participant prefers emailing the course organiser or using a discussion board, indicating that feedback is most useful when it can be communicated quickly through channels where action can be taken.
quote: "if i have, like, any urgent things that need to be fixed, i will just email the course organizer, or through some discussion board, you know, piazza."

explanation: Student describes exhaustion and reduced motivation caused by long days and commuting difficulties, but this does not relate directly to feedback on academic performance or improvement.
quote: "i enter vet school when the sun's down, i'm leaving school when the sun's down... week nine everyone's motivation to go to school just drops immensely... you start missing buses, buses start being twenty minutes late... and people just stop going to school."

code: Attendance reminders perceived as passive aggressive
explanation: Student refers to university emails requiring attendance as negatively toned, but these are attendance communications rather than constructive feedback against learning goals.
quote: "we kind of like, get passive aggressive emails like ‘you have to go to class’"

explanation: The mention of 100% attendance required concerns institutional expectations rather than feedback quality, so it is not thematically relevant to the feedback-focused themes.
quote: "100% attendance required."

explanation: The participant suggests that relying on only one method for giving feedback may exclude students with different personalities, comfort levels, or assumptions about how feedback is received. This aligns with feedback being user-friendly and accessible to different learners/users.
quote: “maybe if people may live a ton of different types of ways that feedback could be given, then, maybe there'd be something for everyone. but it's really only one way to give feedback right now.”

explanation: The participant describes students feeling anxious even when feedback is anonymous, especially if it may be received by a course organiser. This indicates a barrier to engaging with feedback processes, though it is not directly about the quality of feedback itself.
quote: “you're like, you know, it's anonymous, you're still kind of freaked out... they're even more freaked out about that with like an actual course organizer, like receiving it.”
subtheme: Psychological safety and trust in the feedback process

code: Perceived lack of action discourages feedback
explanation: The participant explains that students may not provide feedback if they believe nothing useful or actionable will result from it. This reflects the importance of feedback leading to concrete changes or visible action.
quote: “nothing's really going to be actionable from here. so why bother giving it.”
subtheme: Visible impact and closing the feedback loop

explanation: The participant indicates uncertainty about what their feedback is meant to achieve, suggesting that the goal or purpose of the feedback process is not clear to them.
quote: “i can't answer because like i said, what's the point? i don't know what i'm doing by answering this feedback.”
subtheme: Clarity of purpose and expected outcomes

explanation: The participant suggests that even when feedback indicates something should be changed, the change or its effect is not always visible to the learner, limiting the transparency of feedback.
quote: when given something to change, sometimes you don't always notice the change.

explanation: The participant describes feeling flustered and uncertain about the purpose or role of the feedback, implying that the feedback was not presented in an accessible or learner-friendly way and may have been overwhelming.
quote: just feel quite flustered sometimes... i didn't really know what's its role... a lot of kind of online.
subtheme: Clarity and accessibility of feedback delivery

explanation: The student values staff actively engaging with submitted feedback rather than repeatedly collecting it without visible response. This suggests feedback processes are more meaningful when there is a visible loop between comments and action.
quote: “they were actually engaging with what people had said, rather than kind of just each mid semester and every semester asking for more and more feedback.”

explanation: The student describes appreciating when teachers explicitly communicated how feedback was being used, including what would be changed in future or what had already been considered. This makes the feedback process visible and understandable.
quote: “it was really nice to see the teachers responding to the feedback ... saying, like, ‘oh, this is what we're working on for next year’, or like, ‘we took this into consideration this year’”

explanation: The student highlights that feedback was most valuable when it was acted on within the same semester, allowing students to see the effect of their input while still enrolled in the course.
quote: “in the same semester, the feedback from the midterm surveys were implemented and we saw the difference”

code: Difficulty accessing student representative communication channels
explanation: The participant describes uncertainty and difficulty around how students can contact representatives or raise issues, suggesting a communication-system problem rather than a direct comment on the quality of academic feedback.
quote: “i think it’s a very tricky system… i constantly had to ask the course secretary to post emails on my behalf, so that other students were able to get in contact with me if there was any issues… they should be able to post or have like, learn, a specific area for reps”

explanation: The participant describes how they found out about the session through a mature students WhatsApp group. This is contextual information and does not address qualities of good feedback to students.
quote: for me, i found it out, i guess someone posted it in the mature students whatsapp group.

explanation: The moderator asks participants to recall a time they gave feedback to the university. This sets up the topic but does not itself provide student views on what makes feedback effective.
quote: can you tell us a time that you give a feedback to university? at any level? or any course or department or school?

code: Concerns about free-riding in group work
explanation: The participant describes anxiety and frustration about group members not contributing equally, particularly when group work carries a high proportion of the grade. This relates to assessment experience but does not directly address qualities of feedback.
quote: “i have this fear of having a free rider or someone who's not willing to just put in effort or work... i feel like individual is still better anytime, and if you're giving group work, don't make it 50% of your grade.”
subtheme: Fairness and accountability in group assessment

code: Non-attendance and disrespect for group members’ time
explanation: The participant gives an example of agreed group meetings where members fail to attend, creating difficulties for collaboration. This is relevant to group-work experience rather than feedback from the University.
quote: “we agree on a specific time. and then nobody turns up. so it’s just like, ‘okay, well, shall i do it by myself?’”
subtheme: Fairness and accountability in group assessment

explanation: The participant suggests group work should count for a lower percentage of the final grade because unequal contribution can unfairly affect individual outcomes. This concerns assessment design, not the nature of effective feedback.
quote: “i also want to learn teamworking skills. but 50% of your grade, like, no, i feel like that's also a lot.”

explanation: The student describes uncertainty about who holds authority in the university and how students can connect with decision-makers, indicating a need for clearer and more accessible feedback pathways.
quote: "i feel as if you want to have an agent in the higher authorities in the university and students as we are because i don't know what till what level the authority goes in university here... i don't know how it works in edinburgh university"

explanation: The student appreciates being asked for their opinions and feels cared for, suggesting that soliciting feedback can positively affect students when it is experienced as genuine engagement.
quote: "it's not bad. i like that i'm being asked about, you know, my opinions and how i feel. it's nice, i feel cared for."

explanation: The student questions whether feedback communication is genuinely reciprocal, highlighting the importance of a feedback process where students receive responses and not only provide input.
quote: "but i also feel like okay, is it really is the communication in two ways? or is it balanced?"

explanation: The student wants to know what will happen as a result of the feedback they give, indicating that feedback processes need visible outcomes so students can understand the impact of their contribution.
quote: "i will give all my time and energy to give this feedback, but what is really going to come back to me, so it's a bit what is the point?"

explanation: The student links the university’s response to their feedback with their overall experience, suggesting that feedback is most meaningful when it leads to adjustments that improve future experience.
quote: "the way the university responds to my feedback is going to shape my experience here."

code: Lack of visibility on survey impact
explanation: The participant expresses uncertainty about whether survey responses are seen or acted upon, indicating a need for greater transparency about what happens to feedback once it is provided.
quote: "they did that survey too. but they didn't. i mean, we have no way of knowing if that stuff is actually"

explanation: The participant describes a staff-led session shortly after an exam to review how the paper went, suggesting feedback was provided while the assessment experience was still relatively fresh.
quote: "just before one of our exams sessions as like farm animal feedback session after the exam, just to review how the paper went"

explanation: Staff explicitly reported back on issues raised previously and explained what changes were being made, making the response to student feedback visible and understandable.
quote: "they also just mentioned, this was the stuff that was mentioned last semester, these are the changes we're making with it, which was really nice"

explanation: The participant identifies that student concerns about bus services were recognised by the university and resulted in meetings and progress, indicating feedback was acted upon rather than merely collected.
quote: "a lot of students gave feedback and just how horrible the bus services were... the university did contact us and they did let me sit in two meetings with them and there has been progress in terms of changes"

explanation: The participant contrasts previous experiences with a perceived shift toward listening to students and making improvements, reflecting an ongoing feedback and improvement process.
quote: "it feels like we've evolved more into let’s listen to the students rather than just coming up with stuff"

explanation: Students appear to use both course-level and individual routes to provide feedback, especially when issues are broader or more problematic, indicating a system where feedback can be repeatedly submitted across contexts.
quote: "we also do tend to send a lot of feedback to the dvs here, like individual students will send if it's more problematic matter, which is less than a course level base, but more just the university and how they're doing"

explanation: The student notes a practical facilities issue has been reasonable, but this does not relate to feedback on learning or assessment.
quote: "but everything's been reasonable. like recently the printer is actually on."

explanation: The student describes receiving a dismissive response to a problem with a banging door. The response gives no concrete remedy or next step, illustrating feedback/communication that does not help the student understand what can be changed.
quote: "they're like, we can't do anything about that. and i was like, you could, you just don't want to."

explanation: The student experiences the accommodation team’s response as lacking sympathy and explanation. The issue is observable and specific, but the response does not make clear why action cannot be taken or what evidence informs that decision.
quote: "there's literally no sympathy. we just can't do anything about that."

explanation: The student gave detailed feedback to an RA, but is unsure how it will be implemented or managed. This reflects a need for transparent processes after feedback is submitted.
quote: "i know i've given the feedback, but the implementation of it is going to be very weird"

explanation: The student wants a clearer, more effective system for managing serious flatmate-related concerns after feedback has been given, including how the issue will be followed up and navigated over time.
quote: "so i don't know how it's going to get navigated. and and i wish they had better systems to navigate this."

explanation: The participant seeks clarification about whether the question concerns embarrassment or barriers to giving feedback, but no substantive barrier or feature of effective feedback is described in this excerpt.
quote: s2 41:44: "am i embarrassed about giving feedback?"; second moderator 41:47: "do you have any barriers? or anything stopping you?"
subtheme: Procedural clarification without substantive feedback content

explanation: The participant suggests that knowing professors and attending in-person lectures creates more interaction, which in turn increases the amount of feedback students receive.
quote: “definitely knowing professors, going to in-person lectures, and having interaction would mean increased feedback.”

code: Early clarification reduces need for major later feedback
explanation: The participant contrasts in-person interaction with online learning, implying that regular clarification and minor adjustments can prevent the need for more substantial feedback later.
quote: “it would reduce the amount of major feedback and slight changes that people want to see or like, clarifications, versus when it was online, when people would have more significant feedback, recommendations, because it's like, they didn't really have that interaction.”

explanation: The excerpt discusses study logistics, budget constraints, campus selection, and participant turnout across schools rather than features of good feedback to students.

explanation: The participant provides introductory demographic/course information, but this does not address qualities of good feedback to students.

explanation: The moderator asks how the participant found out about the feedback network/sign-up sheet, but no response is provided in the excerpt and it does not contain substantive data about feedback quality.

explanation: Feedback opportunities are made easy to access through QR codes shown around lectures, suggesting a clear and convenient mechanism for students to provide responses.

explanation: Survey questions created by student representatives were experienced as more useful than staff-generated questions, implying that feedback processes are clearer and more relevant when framed in terms students understand.

code: Embedding feedback opportunities into key teaching moments
explanation: Placing the survey between important lectures increased participation because students were already present and likely to engage, showing the value of integrating feedback opportunities into the learning routine.

explanation: Elected student representatives gather information from each year group about teaching and course experience, indicating an organised structure for collecting feedback across the programme.

explanation: The participant expresses dissatisfaction and distrust toward the university’s motives, suggesting the course structure may be driven by financial gain from international students rather than educational quality. This does not directly address characteristics of good feedback.

explanation: The participant indicates frustration that course activities could have been conducted face to face. Although this relates to learning experience, it does not specifically concern feedback practices.

explanation: The speakers discuss the size and demographic composition of the cohort, particularly the proportion of international and Indian students. This is not thematically relevant to feedback quality.

code: Unable to compare course experience across years
explanation: The participant states they cannot evaluate whether the course has improved because they have no experience of the course in previous years or at another year level. This does not address characteristics of good feedback, so it is coded as undefined.

explanation: The extract references a desire for a more streamlined feedback mechanism, suggesting that existing processes may feel complex or difficult to navigate. However, the quote is indirect and does not provide detail about academic feedback to students.

explanation: The participant raises concerns about whether students at non-main campuses struggle to contact people at the main university or feel heard. explanation: The participant values feedback from the University that clearly communicates how student comments have been received and what the institution will do in response.

explanation: Good feedback is described as constructive when it identifies concrete short-term actions and longer-term priorities, rather than giving a vague acknowledgement.

explanation: The participant highlights the importance of changes being implemented immediately where possible, suggesting that rapid response increases the value of feedback.

explanation: The participant stresses that students need evidence that their contributions are listened to, rather than feeling that reviews are meaningless or ignored.

explanation: The lecturer’s use of the top three student videos made high-performing work visible to the cohort. This functions as a concrete, observable example of what successful performance can look like, although the extract does not indicate whether criteria were explicitly discussed.
quote: “their assignment was just sending a video... what the lecturer did was that he said to them that the top three videos will be shown... ‘three, two, one. and we'll show you the winners’.”

explanation: The student suggests that making feedback or assessment-related sessions engaging and anticipatory can increase attendance, even late in the term. quote: “everyone turned out for that seminar... it was week eight... everyone’s so swamped with work... and the fact that... everyone turned up... that’s amazing.”

explanation: The extract highlights that students may attend because the session includes recognition, competition, or something enjoyable to look forward to. This concerns engagement with teaching activities more than the qualities of effective feedback.

code: Choice between in-person and anonymous feedback
explanation: Students value being able to decide whether to give feedback face-to-face or anonymously, suggesting that effective systems should accommodate different preferences and reduce barriers to participation.

explanation: The participant is motivated to give feedback because they want the university to recognise that students are experiencing a genuine issue, implying that acknowledgement is important even before changes are made.

explanation: The participant frames engagement with university processes and work as primarily dependent on the student, rather than something the university can compel. explanation: The participant suggests the university does not provide many resources for students, but the extract does not specify feedback quality, timing, clarity, actionability, or consistency in relation to feedback given to students.

explanation: The participant indicates that feedback should occur more regularly than only one or two times per semester, suggesting value in repeated feedback opportunities.

explanation: The participant appears to discuss giving feedback and possible consequences, but the excerpt is incomplete and does not clearly relate to the qualities of good feedback to students.

explanation: The participant suggests they would be much more willing to complete surveys if they could see that previous feedback had led to actual changes, indicating the importance of a visible feedback-action cycle.

explanation: The participant explains that some students may attend teaching sessions but still not share feedback because they are too shy, meaning collected feedback may not be a true reflection of student views. explanation: The participant identifies multiple groups whose views may be missing or overrepresented, suggesting institutional feedback may be biased toward students who attend, are satisfied, or feel confident speaking. explanation: The participant describes feedback or university practices as being justified only by tradition rather than a clear explanation, indicating a perceived lack of transparency about why things are done in a particular way.

explanation: The participant describes feeling separated from the central campus, particularly in relation to sports clubs and access to university sports events. This does not relate to the qualities of academic feedback, so it is coded as undefined.

explanation: The participant describes uncertainty about whether student feedback is read or acted upon, suggesting that feedback processes need to be transparent so students can see the outcome or impact of their contributions.

code: Feedback perceived as pointless without response
explanation: The participant indicates that when students cannot see whether feedback leads to change, they may feel the process is not worthwhile. This reflects the importance of an ongoing cycle where feedback is acknowledged, acted upon, and communicated back to learners.

explanation: The excerpt contains only moderator coordination about ending the interview recording and does not provide substantive data about what makes good feedback to students.

explanation: The participant is unsure whether previous in-person interactions count as feedback, describing them as informal. This does not provide a clear view on what makes feedback effective, so it is not thematically aligned with the specified feedback quality themes.

so every feedback you've given, has just nothing's been done with it, basically.

explanation: The participant’s example involves lack of lecture slides and recordings, which created accessibility concerns. Their intervention made materials more visible and accessible to students, highlighting the value of transparent and available learning resources.
quote: “a lecturer… refuses to provide lecture slides, or record his lectures… that goes against the disability act… i collected all the slides, recorded all the lectures, put everything in order, and segmented the recordings.”

explanation: The moderator interprets the example as showing a situation where an authority figure was non-responsive, prompting student intervention. This reflects a breakdown in feedback responsiveness, although it is more about institutional response to student feedback than direct feedback to learners.
quote: “often feedback ends up being like, non-responsive, and here, there was a situation where there was sort of a non-responsive authority figure and you were like, i'm going to intervene.”
subtheme: Responsiveness and trust in feedback processes

code: Equality of voices in feedback systems
explanation: The moderator raises whether existing feedback systems allow all student voices to be heard equally. This concerns inclusivity of feedback collection rather than the characteristics of good feedback given to students.
quote: “trying to think about voices… all voices… equality of voices… whether or not the feedback systems that exist allow for all voices to be heard.”

explanation: Students indicate that email is not an effective or accessible channel for university communication because they receive too many emails and may not open them, which could reduce the likelihood that feedback is noticed or used.
quote: "i never open emails. like if i can avoid it" / "email's not a good way of communicating with us. just because we get so many of them, there's just no point."

explanation: Current student feedback methods are perceived as biased toward students who already attend, engage with, understand, or enjoy the course, meaning their views may dominate feedback data.
quote: i feel like it's kind of biased towards people who are already engaging with the course. and maybe it's like, they like the material in the course and they understand what's going on.

explanation: Students who are struggling may be less likely to provide feedback because they lack time or motivation, or do not see feedback forms as useful for improving their understanding.
quote: whereas people who might be really struggling with the course, like, don't have the time or the motivation to fill out feedback forms for it. or they feel like it's not going to help them understand it more.

explanation: Feedback collected from students present in class may disproportionately reflect the perspectives of those already interested and invested in the module, rather than the wider student cohort.
quote: most of the people who filled the results for our classes were in the classes themselves. so they obviously had a bias that like, they were there, were wanting to study and they actually had an interest in learning more about that specific class and topics.

explanation: The participant suggests tutors should ask students for feedback at the end of the final tutorial. This concerns students giving feedback to the university rather than what makes feedback from the university to students effective, so it is not thematically relevant to the provided feedback-quality themes.
quote: “maybe in the last tutorial, it would be a good idea. at the end, even if it's not individual, just ask if anyone has any feedback.”

explanation: The exchange identifies that midterm feedback is completed online, but it does not provide detail about effective feedback to students or qualities such as timing, actionability, clarity, or consistency.
quote: “when you fill out the midterm feedback, is that online?” / “yeah.”

explanation: Feedback was collected at mid-semester, suggesting a timing point when the course is still underway and there may still be opportunity for the university or course team to respond.
quote: "i've only had to give feedback at the mid semester"

explanation: The feedback was gathered through a provided form, indicating a structured and accessible mechanism for communicating feedback rather than an informal or unclear process.
quote: "they just kept the feedback on the form that was sent to us"

explanation: The student did not need to actively seek out a way to provide feedback, implying that the process was made available to them and did not require additional effort beyond completing the requested form.
quote: "but i haven't had to go out of my way to give feedback"

explanation: The participant notes that this is their first semester and they have only provided feedback when required, which limits the relevance of the extract to detailed features of effective feedback.
quote: "given that this is my first semester in this school"

explanation: The student frames effective support/feedback as involving opportunities to ask questions about assignments, contrasting a refusal to answer essay questions with a course organiser offering Q&A sessions.
quote: literally one course organiser said i can't even email her question about the essay... then the other course organizers said like, okay, i'm thinking of doing like a q&a, which is at least... she's doing two of them

explanation: Effective feedback is associated with course organisers showing genuine interest in responding to students and improving the course, rather than being unavailable or dismissive.
quote: it's about the course i have, course organisers actually showing interest in making that change.

explanation: The student emphasises being kept involved in a process where feedback is requested and used to make improvements, suggesting feedback should be part of an iterative dialogue.
quote: even as involved in the loop that, oh, we are interested in making the change, you just need to show you need to give us suggestions on how to make that better or smoother.

explanation: The participant/moderator suggests that students may be less motivated to complete feedback forms if they do not believe their comments will be heard or lead to future changes. This concerns institutional responsiveness to student feedback rather than the qualities of feedback given to students.
quote: "there has to be some sort of incentive laid out in the sense that at least you should feel that your voices heard and that what you say is going to actually be... implemented in the future"

explanation: The form-based feedback process is described as feeling impersonal, which may discourage engagement. The excerpt does not directly address feedback provided to students on their learning or performance.
quote: "yeah, probably like you're saying it feels quite impersonal in a way."

code: Feedback should identify what to preserve
explanation: The participant notes that feedback often focuses on what needs changing, but positive elements are also important because they signal what should remain the same in future. This reflects feedback that is actionable by clarifying both what to change and what to repeat.
quote: "when you're giving feedback, you're like, well, what do i want to change? and the things that are good, you really don't want to change? maybe a lot of people don't think to mention it."
subtheme: Identifying what to maintain as well as change

explanation: The participant describes negative or improvement-focused points as easier to identify than strengths, suggesting feedback processes may naturally prioritise problems over reinforcing successful practice.
quote: "there seems like a lot more sort of obvious, the things that i want to change opposed to the things that i'm happy the way they are."
subtheme: Identifying what to maintain as well as change

code: Feedback discussion signposted through course experience
explanation: The participant explains that students are told course feedback will be discussed, and that longer-term familiarity with the vet school helps them understand what this means. This suggests feedback processes are embedded and repeated over time, though perhaps relying partly on students’ prior experience.
quote: "they did mention that they will be going through a bit of the front course feedback... but just because we've been in vet school for so long, we kind of know that means that they would mention it a little bit"

code: Problems raised by students are acknowledged
explanation: The participant indicates that staff tend to mention the issues or problems received from students when discussing feedback, showing that feedback is linked to observable student concerns, although the detail of resulting action is unclear.
quote: "they would mention it a little bit, at least in terms of the problems that they received from us"

explanation: The discussion concerns paper-based midterm feedback forms/evaluations that students filled in during lectures, rather than feedback from the University on students’ academic performance. Therefore it is not directly relevant to the provided feedback-to-students themes.
quote: “do they still do midterm paper feedback? ... we got little papers. and you could just put it right... you got it at the beginning of the lecture... [s2: i had that in first year, but no, it stopped] ... i loved that, though.”

explanation: The student is unsure who receives student feedback, suggesting limited transparency about the feedback process and where comments are directed.
quote: i'm not too sure where the feedback goes, either. but i think it goes to the course organiser

explanation: Some courses shared the results of student feedback and explained how staff would improve, making the impact of students' feedback visible and understandable.
quote: after we had feedback, we had, like 10 minutes spent on the results of the feedback and how they would do better.

explanation: A student request for more live interaction was implemented soon after being raised, showing feedback being used promptly while still relevant to the course experience.
quote: there's demand for more live interaction... and that was put into place pretty soon

explanation: The course responded to feedback by adding an online lecture or Q&A session, demonstrating a concrete change based on learner input.
quote: we had an online lecture for three weeks, like, more of a q&a session, that was put up.

explanation: The student does not understand how peer moderation marks are calculated or interpreted, making the feedback/assessment process feel opaque and difficult to trust.
quote: "i'm still trying to work out how it works in here... i got the lowest score. so, i'm wondering how it works."
subtheme: Clarity of assessment processes and consequences

code: Fear of penalty for honest peer feedback
explanation: The student worries that marking a non-contributing peer accurately may be interpreted negatively against them, suggesting the criteria are not stable or reliably understood.
quote: "if you mark them low, they will say that you cannot work as a team... i could penalise in a way for telling the truth. so, it's a bit of a grey area. i don't know what to do"
subtheme: Trust and fairness in peer assessment

explanation: The student compares their previous undergraduate experience, where the consequence of peer marks was clear, with the current situation where the impact on grades is uncertain.
quote: "back in my undergrad, if we had a free rider, we could mark that here. and then the professor would deduct marks if the accumulative mark is lower than a certain percentage."
subtheme: Clarity of assessment processes and consequences

explanation: The speaker describes peer moderation as encouraging game-like behaviour, where students may give full marks or mark others down strategically rather than evaluating contribution against shared criteria.
quote: "it's like... is he gonna mark me full marks or is he gonna mark me down? if he's gonna mark me down. i'm gonna mark him down. but how am i supposed to know he's gonna mark me down?"
subtheme: Trust and fairness in peer assessment

explanation: The speaker suggests that even when contribution levels differ, students may agree to give everyone full marks to avoid negative consequences, reducing the usefulness of feedback about actual performance.
quote: "even if one person didn’t do that much work... we don't try to agree to mark everyone full marks just in case these stuff happens."

explanation: The excerpt contains only moderators setting up the interview activity and asking the participant to introduce themselves and discuss drawings; it does not provide substantive data about what makes feedback good.
quote: "please introduce yourself. and we're going to do something about the drawings."

code: Perceived unfair grading across tutorial groups
explanation: The student reports that their tutorial group believes they were graded unfairly compared with other groups, indicating concern that marking and feedback criteria may not be applied reliably or consistently across markers.
quote: "one of my tutorial groups is doing a mass complaint against our tutor right now, because we were graded unfairly in proportion to like the marks that everyone in other groups got."

code: Moderation not yet available for midterm marks
explanation: The discussion notes that moderation has not yet returned for the midterm, suggesting that checks on marking consistency are delayed or absent at the point when students are reacting to their feedback or marks.
quote: "wasn't it moderated?" / "the moderation hasn’t come back yet, because it’s a midterm."

explanation: The student describes discomfort with being directed first to the original marker when disputing feedback or a mark. This relates to the institutional process around feedback disputes rather than a specific quality of the feedback itself.
quote: "if you disagree with, like your feedback, or your mark, or something, the first place they tell you to go is to the marker, which i feel like can be really intimidating."
subtheme: Accessible and psychologically safe appeals processes

explanation: The participant describes not knowing all peers due to the size of the course, which relates to the broader student learning experience but does not address feedback practices.
quote: i don't even know all my peers, let's put it that way.
subtheme: Cohort Size and Impersonal Learning Environment

explanation: The participant reports that classroom space was insufficient for the number of students, causing inconvenience and affecting the learning environment, but this is not thematically relevant to feedback quality.
quote: it couldn't accommodate all of us and we had to sit in chairs where didn't have to let the laptop table ,and that was yeah it was very inconvenient.

explanation: The student values that the teaching team responded quickly after students raised concerns, suggesting timely feedback or institutional response is viewed positively because it shows concerns are heard while the course is still ongoing.
quote: “so we gave that feedback. and like, the response was immediate.”

explanation: The student is impressed that changes were made in the short term, indicating that feedback is experienced as more effective when it leads to visible action soon enough to affect the current learning experience.
quote: “actually, they have really done the short term. that really impressed me.”

code: Lack of upfront clarity about teaching format
explanation: Students felt they were not clearly informed when enrolling that most sessions would be taught by tutors rather than lecturers, highlighting the importance of transparent communication about course delivery and expectations.
quote: “when we signed up for this course, we were not aware that our most of our classes are going to be with tutors. they are tutors, not lecturers, they are phd students.”
subtheme: Clarity of expectations and course delivery

code: Feedback enables adjustment during the unit
explanation: The discussion suggests that students gave feedback while the course was running and the teaching team adjusted provision, reflecting feedback as part of an ongoing improvement cycle rather than only end-of-course evaluation.
quote: “we gave that feedback. and like, the response was immediate. and now the senior teaching fellows…”

explanation: The participant describes receiving too many emails to manage, suggesting that communication from the tutor may be overwhelming rather than accessible or manageable for the learner.
quote: "one of my personal tutors treat me like that. but there's like, i get way too many emails. i can't respond."

explanation: The participant expresses resentment about feeling that work is being pushed onto them and that they must sacrifice other things. This reflects a general burden of university demands, but it is not clearly about feedback specifically.
quote: "resentment, like a little bit of like, you're pushing all this work on me. yeah. and i kind of have to sacrifice some things."

explanation: The participant describes frustration that the university asks students for feedback but does not provide a meaningful response, suggesting a broken feedback loop where students cannot see whether their input has led to action.
quote: the unit always asked for our feedback, but then like, you never get any response to it really

explanation: The participant indicates that when responses to feedback are postponed, they lose usefulness and relevance, highlighting the importance of timely communication while the issue still matters.
quote: it's like, postponed, it irrelevant anymore. and that's frustrating.
subtheme: Feedback must be timely to remain useful

code: Resource access barriers during hybrid learning
explanation: The participant describes being unable to access physical learning resources such as artworks and books, which affected motivation. This relates to broader learning experience rather than characteristics of good feedback from the University.
quote: “there's a lot where we have to look at actual pieces or just read books and and everything like that. and so we weren't able to access anything from that. yeah, and it just became really hard to stay motivated”
subtheme: Access to learning resources and study conditions

explanation: The student wants their feedback to be heard by someone who can respond, and expects the University to show students that it is acting on concerns rather than deflecting responsibility.
quote: "i want my feedback to be told to somebody, so i can have a good university experience... at least try to, like negotiate with lothian buses and they come back to students... give students like the reassurance that okay, the university is here for people, for students"

code: Feedback should lead to concrete action
explanation: The student frames good feedback as something that results in practical institutional action, such as negotiation with transport providers, rather than simply saying nothing can be done.
quote: "we can't do it because it's like a different institution... if you can't like at least try to, like negotiate with lothian buses"

explanation: The student identifies monthly town hall meetings as a recurring channel through which student feedback and institutional responses may be communicated.
quote: "i think monthly, we get town hall meeting."

explanation: The student describes institutional responses as dismissive or unable to address concerns, which does not clearly fit the positive feedback qualities except as a general dissatisfaction with the feedback process.
quote: "people will just keep shoving like... we can't do it because it's like a different institution. like it's literally busus: i can't do anything; the university can’t do anything."

explanation: The participant suggests that feedback is easier to provide when respondents can select from predefined options, such as scales or sliders, rather than being required to write extensive free text. This highlights the importance of making feedback processes accessible and low-burden for the user.
quote: "it's always easier when there's like different options, or just to have to point and choose, rather than having to write loads in all cases... i would put more like, likert scales, where you just have to choose or slide."

explanation: The participant values having an optional text box for additional detail, allowing respondents to expand only when they feel it is necessary. This suggests feedback systems should avoid overwhelming users while still permitting richer input.
quote: "and then put the box for text. and just fill that in if you want to... if the respondent wants to answer more, they can just do that in the text box."

code: Delayed feedback structures in short course
explanation: The student frames the absence of early feedback or response mechanisms as especially problematic because the programme is short, meaning delays quickly reduce usefulness and create a sense that time is being wasted.
quote: "it's a very short program... we only have 10 weeks this semester... by the second week, nothing was happening. and there's only eight weeks left... it's a waste of time."
subtheme: Early feedback mechanisms in compressed programmes

explanation: The student notes that student representatives were only in place a month into the course, limiting the speed with which student concerns could be communicated and addressed.
quote: "the student rep thing happened only a month into the course. so we didn't have any student reps till then."
subtheme: Early feedback mechanisms in compressed programmes

explanation: Students created an Excel sheet to gather and document specific issues, making feedback more visible, organised, and evidence-based before presenting it through representatives.
quote: "some people proactively made like an excel sheet and everyone was like, okay, get in there, put down whatever issues you have."

explanation: The student identifies increased direct contact with professors as a desirable improvement, suggesting feedback and communication are more effective when students can access academic staff directly.
quote: "I put it down on the excel sheet that, you know, having more contact with the professor's directly would be nice."

explanation: The student recognises that individualised attention is unrealistic in a large class and that students need to adapt, implying feedback processes must be manageable and appropriate to the learning context.
quote: "you can't get individualized attention... that's just not going to be possible, especially when you have 160 people in the class. so there is some amount of adaptation that you need to go through."

explanation: The collected issues were prepared for student representatives to take forward, showing feedback becoming concrete and directed toward an institutional response.
quote: "by the time they were ready, they already had the excel sheet ready to go to the proposal."

explanation: The excerpt contains only procedural setup, participant introductions, degree information, and how participants found out about the study. It does not discuss student feedback or qualities of good feedback.
quote: "i'm s5, i studied chemistry in second year, and i found out about it through an email..." / "hi, i'm s4. i'm studying science and math. and i was found out by email."

explanation: The participant agrees that students need clearer information about what general feedback looks like and what actions are being taken in response, reflecting the importance of making feedback processes visible and understandable.
quote: "so just more transparency, you think, in terms of letting students know what general feedback is like and what's being done to implement it?" / "yeah."

explanation: Repeated survey emails are experienced as excessive and performative, leading students to ignore them rather than engage. This relates to feedback processes becoming less effective when communication is not manageable or meaningful for students.
quote: "with getting so many emails about the same survey, most people will start to disregard it, i've started to disregard it, because it seems like it's almost become just like a show to send it out."

explanation: The participant suggests that feedback requests may be more effective if they occur less often, such as once a semester or once a year, so that they feel more purposeful and are less likely to be ignored.
quote: "instead, maybe once a semester, once a year, even, just to make it more of a rare occasion."

explanation: The participant describes a lack of transparency after students submit feedback through forms, noting that they rarely know what happens to it or whether any action is taken.
quote: “we might share it, but then we don't know what's happening with it… if it's a form, that you're just filling in, i think rarely i've known what's actually done with that.”

explanation: The participant contrasts anonymous or formal feedback mechanisms with emailing lecturers directly, where students are more likely to receive a visible response and understand that their concern has been seen.
quote: “if you maybe say that directly yourself… throw an email directly to a lecturer… you might actually see it because they will get back to you.”

explanation: The student emphasises that when they raise issues, they want concrete guidance or possible solutions rather than a simple refusal or statement that the university cannot help.
quote: “what we don't want to hear that is, ‘we cannot solve this issue’ or ‘sorry, we cannot help with that’. rather than like, ‘in order to solve this issue, what you need to do is blah, blah, blah’”

explanation: The participant values feedback or support that outlines what the school will do, including possible options, so students can understand how the issue may be addressed.
quote: “what we are gonna do is probably solution one, solution two, solution three’, rather than like just saying ‘we cannot do it’.

code: Students seek institutional help for unsolved problems
explanation: The participant suggests that students approach the school because they believe it has the capacity to help with issues students cannot resolve alone, implying feedback should acknowledge this and provide meaningful direction.
quote: “if a student is asking the school for help, probably they think the school has the power to solve it, or they themselves cannot solve the issue.”

explanation: The participant describes temporarily giving deliberately low satisfaction scores as a joke before correcting them, which relates to survey behaviour rather than substantive characteristics of effective feedback.
quote: "i will just joke by giving everything like the lowest score, and like, show it to my classmate. but i will correct it before i submit it."

explanation: The participant emphasises that feedback is valuable when students can see that it has been heard and translated into concrete changes, rather than disappearing without acknowledgement.
quote: “there's a lot of times where i feel like the need for the teaching staff to go ‘we've heard your feedback. and this is what we've done to help like the students and stuff. i feel like we don't get that enough.”

code: Feedback influencing curriculum but not welfare
explanation: The participant distinguishes between feedback being used for curriculum change and a perceived lack of action on feedback about student welfare and belonging.
quote: “a lot of this feedback is contributed to changing the curriculum and everything, but not a lot of it is being directed towards that student welfare and how to integrate that in our campus, making us all feel more like at home.”

explanation: The participant describes an early period where the course felt disorganised, which influenced students' overall impressions and made them more critical of the course. This does not directly address qualities of effective feedback to students, so it is coded as undefined.
quote: "everything's a little disorganized. at the beginning, i feel like people have this impression, and that it colored everything else that we're seeing. and it was like, people kind of got judgy with the course."

code: Feedback too lengthy to engage with
explanation: The participant identifies overly long feedback as a barrier because students may not have enough time to read or process it. This suggests effective feedback should be concise and manageable rather than overwhelming.
quote: "i agree when they are too long because it's not like we have too much time to sit there"

code: Questioning whether feedback leads to change
explanation: The participant questions whether engaging with lengthy feedback would actually result in improvement, implying concern about whether feedback produces useful change for future work.
quote: "even if you had the time would things change?"

explanation: The exchange identifies tools used for class interaction or polling, but it does not provide substantive detail about the quality, timing, clarity, actionability, or consistency of feedback to students.
quote: primary moderator: "you do know piazza? so i think business school use something called a discussion forum, right?" / s1: "we use qualtric."

code: Low response rate limits feedback availability
explanation: The participant notes that only a small proportion of students responded, making it difficult to obtain sufficient feedback. This is about feedback collection challenges rather than qualities of effective feedback to students, so it is not directly aligned with the main feedback-quality themes.
quote: "let's just say 100. but then we got about 21 responses back so it is difficult to get feedback."

explanation: The participant distinguishes between good responses and very simple yes/no answers, suggesting that feedback is less useful when it lacks detail or constructive content. This aligns with the need for feedback to be concrete and usable rather than minimal or evaluative only.
quote: "yeah, they were good. but some of them are again, basically, just like simple ‘yes’ or ‘no’ question... they sometimes they don't want to think how they can give constructive feedback."

explanation: The participant suggests that end-of-semester feedback may be preferable because students are focused on deadlines and may not have capacity to provide thoughtful responses earlier. This relates to timing feedback so it can be given when participants are more able to engage with it.
quote: "because they're so focused on other things like getting their deadlines... so i think maybe that's why i think doing feedback at the end of the semester is a better idea."

explanation: The student describes disengaging from feedback surveys due to fatigue, despite recognising that this may reduce the likelihood of their views being represented. This concerns student-to-university feedback mechanisms rather than feedback given to students on their learning, so it is not directly aligned with the provided feedback-quality themes.
quote: "it's just the whole thing of survey fatigue? like, i'm just tired of filling them out. so i just don't anymore, which i know is bad, because it makes my voice not be heard,but, like, it’s not the priority."

explanation: The student questions what it actually means for their voice to be heard, suggesting uncertainty about whether giving feedback leads to meaningful response or change. However, the focus is institutional listening rather than educational feedback to improve student performance.
quote: "yeah, like, what does it mean to have your voice heard? like, what does it actually mean?"

explanation: The moderator summarises a contrast between limited formal school-level conversation and greater opportunities for dialogue through societies. This relates to channels for student representation rather than the characteristics of academic feedback to students.
quote: "your school didn’t give a lot of opportunity for you to have a conversation with them. but the societies, you have the approach and the opportunities to be in the conversation?"
subtheme: Informal and Alternative Channels for Dialogue

explanation: The participant describes being asked to give feedback immediately at an event, but the surrounding distractions and pressure to leave reduce the thoughtfulness and quality of responses. This relates to timing: feedback opportunities need to occur when students can still remember the event but also have enough space to respond carefully.
quote: "they tell you to give them feedback right there, they put the qr on the projector... there's a lot of like stuffs happening around... you're just like quickly... getting through it. so you do not really fill in with full dedication"

code: Feedback process not easy to complete later
explanation: The student reports losing access to the feedback form after scanning the QR code and closing their tabs, meaning they were unable to provide feedback. This highlights the need for feedback systems to be accessible and easy to use, without creating avoidable barriers.
quote: "i scan the qr code, put my phone away, and then i close all the tabs. and it's gone. so i'm not able to provide feedback."

code: Feedback should reach people able to respond
explanation: The participant says course feedback should be read by the course professor and programme representative. This suggests feedback is most useful when directed to people with responsibility or capacity to act on it.
quote: "when i'm giving the feedback, especially when it's for my course, i want my course professor to read it... and the second person should be the programme rep."

explanation: The extract consists of moderators introducing the focus group purpose, consent, anonymity, recording, and the opening prompt. It does not contain participant views about what makes feedback to students effective.
quote: “the purpose of this project is really gives you an opportunity to raise your student feedback… we will recording this session, but audio only… all the names will be anonymous… my first question is, can tell us… about a time when you give feedback to the university…”

explanation: The participant suggests that feedback formats requiring lengthy written responses deter engagement, while simple rating scales with optional comments would be clearer and easier to complete.
quote: "for that feedback for all of the questions are also worthy questions that you have to like, formulate something to say each point which put off people a lot, there's no like, how do you feel on a scale of one to 10 about that. and then you could just go like, tick, tick, tick and add optional comments"
subtheme: Ease and simplicity of giving feedback

explanation: The participant describes the value of having a continuously available general feedback form for each course, allowing students to provide feedback whenever an issue or comment arises rather than only at fixed points.
quote: "it would be good if there was just one, constantly open, sort of general feedback form for me for each course... just like one thing you want to say that you could be able to say at any point in time"

code: Immediate feedback after specific learning activities
explanation: The participant proposes optional quick feedback after workshops or weekly activities, enabling students to comment while the experience is still recent and specific.
quote: "they could just have... a question that you optionally respond to saying like how you felt about a workshop, for example, from one to 10... if you have any, like specific comments"
subtheme: Feedback close to the learning event

code: Specific weekly feedback supports course improvement
explanation: The participant recalls finding weekly optional comments useful because they could identify when a particular week had not been taught well, making feedback tied to a concrete teaching episode.
quote: "at the end of our quizzes... we had like an optional question that was just what are your comments on how this week went? and that was really helpful, because sometimes you actually felt like that week just hadn't been taught well"
subtheme: Concrete feedback linked to specific teaching episodes

code: Lack of accessible route for specific concerns
explanation: The participant notes wanting to give feedback about a particular quiz but feeling there was no suitable mechanism other than email, which they were reluctant to use because it would be personally identifiable.
quote: "i wish they had this because i would say something about this quiz specifically, but they don't. and there's i don't feel like there is actually any way for me to reach out and say... unless i want to email them. but i don't want it to be like tied"

explanation: The participant suggests that if students are told a class is only a feedback session, they may choose not to attend. This concerns engagement with a feedback-related session rather than the quality of feedback itself, so it is only indirectly relevant to the study aims.
quote: "i don't think you should warn students about feedback during the classes, because i know, some students were like, oh, it's just a feedback session. we don't need to go then, so maybe just don’t warn them."

explanation: The moderator raises the idea of offering a small coursework bonus for completing feedback. This appears to refer to encouraging students to fill out feedback rather than describing what makes feedback to students effective.
quote: "what if everyone gets like one per cent bonuses if you fill out this feedback for coursework?"

explanation: The discussion highlights that holding feedback-related activity in the final seminar may be ineffective because students are unlikely to attend due to exams and other pressures. This relates to timing and accessibility of feedback opportunities.
quote: "nobody shows up to the last seminar. yeah, it's like week 11 everyone has like crazy examinations or just in the library - you're not going to a seminar"

explanation: The participant suggests assessment should reflect what was effectively taught and what is valuable within the course, rather than heavily weighting areas where teaching was inadequate. This relates to feedback and assessment being referenced to clear course goals and learner understanding of expected content.
quote: "at least you're getting examined on something that you think is valuable to the course... if you know that majority of the students again, say for our course, pig was not taught really well. you wouldn't put heavy weighted marks on it."
subtheme: Alignment with taught content and course value

explanation: The participant emphasises that concerns about course delivery or exam content should be raised before the exam, with enough time for the university to respond and adjust the paper if needed.
quote: "if you mentioned that before the course before the exam, like enough time to actually have a say on how the papers going."
subtheme: Feedback early enough to influence outcomes

explanation: The participant describes a process where student feedback on poorly taught areas could be used to adapt assessment weighting, showing feedback as part of an improvement cycle rather than something collected too late to matter.
quote: "if you know that majority of the students again, say for our course, pig was not taught really well. you wouldn't put heavy weighted marks on it. because if the course itself is the issue, you can't really hold that against the students"
