explanation: The participant wants feedback to be received, sorted by relevance, and communicated to the people responsible, indicating that effectiveness depends on a transparent and organised feedback pathway.
quote: "having someone who can like take in all the feedback, and then decide which group each bit concerned and make sure that everyone who is involved is informed of the feedback."

explanation: The participant suggests that particularly harsh or personal feedback may need to be moderated before being passed on, reflecting concern that feedback should be communicated in a usable and appropriate way.
quote: "if the feedback is particularly bitter or twisted, maybe not giving us an uncensored to the people involved"

explanation: The participant describes feedback being split into individual courses and general issues so that the relevant staff can respond, showing the value of directing feedback to where action can be taken.
quote: "they’ll split it up into the individual courses... section the main stuff out and then give the general stuff to everyone. and then individually in the course, they found solutions."

explanation: The participant distinguishes between course-specific feedback and wider structural issues, arguing that general problems should be escalated to a higher level where change can happen.
quote: "that stuff, that isn't just one course, that should be given up to a higher place, which i don't know if it's given up"

explanation: The participant feels that concerns about content load should have been addressed earlier, implying that delayed action reduces the usefulness of feedback and leaves students overwhelmed.
quote: "the content load has been something that a lot of people have been talking about, there's something that should have been done last semester... instead of piling it all up now to and we feeling overwhelmed."

explanation: The participant describes formal channels for raising concerns as ineffective or risky, particularly when giving critical feedback to someone senior. This concerns institutional complaint/feedback mechanisms and power dynamics rather than the qualities of academic feedback given to students, so it is not directly aligned with the provided feedback themes.
quote: “you have these channels, but they don’t lead anywhere.” / “someone senior to me, and i need to tell them, your tone of voice that you use for students is deeply unappreciated, i'm not going to be comfortable doing that... they definitely have some possibility of... not accepting my paper or maybe not giving me a promotion or putting me forward for a job.”
subtheme: Psychological safety and power barriers in feedback systems

explanation: The participant suggests feedback is most useful when read by the instructor or course organiser because they have the necessary context to understand and respond to it; escalation is only needed if they are unwilling to act.
quote: i feel like most of the time, the instructor or the course organiser has the most context to actually respond to it. it's only when they don't really want to respond to it, that it makes sense to have it go to someone above them.
subtheme: Directed to those with capacity to act

explanation: The participant proposes making student feedback visible to other students so they can indicate agreement, helping staff see whether an issue is isolated or widespread.
quote: allow other students to read feedback the students are writing. so that if the students also agree with what their course mate is saying, they can kind of support it or like it so that the professor knows... how widespread a certain issue is.

explanation: The participant refers to giving feedback about how tutorials are run and the balance between in-person and online teaching, but provides limited detail about the qualities of the feedback itself.
quote: it's happened to me in a few classes too. on how tutorials are run, for instance, and also about the in-person/online thing that i mentioned earlier with the class.

explanation: The participant emphasises that feedback is valuable when it is implemented and connected back to students’ learning, suggesting a need for a feedback cycle rather than one-off collection.
quote: "like i mean, is implementing the feedback." ... "seeing where it goes and what people then doing about it later on and how that then comes back to you guys in terms of your learning. that's what you want to see."

explanation: The participant wants transparency about what happens after feedback is submitted, including where it goes and what actions are taken as a result.
quote: "actually seeing where it goes and what people then doing about it later on"

explanation: The participant notes that feedback forms may function, but their repetitive nature is a negative feature of the feedback process. This relates more to the experience of completing institutional forms than to the quality of feedback students receive.
quote: "i think that the feedback forms do work at the end of the day, other than them being incredibly repetitive all the time."

explanation: The participant describes receiving multiple, repetitive surveys each semester and being continuously asked to give the same feedback. This concerns students giving feedback to the university rather than receiving feedback from the university, so it is not directly relevant to the specified feedback themes.
quote: “i think we're too many... i received several in a semester... i'm continuously being asked to give feedback, exact same things.”

explanation: The participant prioritises feedback processes where requests or concerns lead to observable action, emphasising that students should be able to see that their feedback has had an effect.
quote: "maybe that the feedback was actually... like what we were asking for was actually done and that we could see that."

explanation: The student distinguishes between generally good email responsiveness across most courses and poor responsiveness in a few, suggesting inconsistency in how students can access clarification or feedback depending on the course or organiser.
quote: “it was that particular course organiser because i knew a few other people had similar problems with their marks. i think most of my courses, they've been pretty good at responding to emails. it's kind of just a few courses that are not run as well.”

code: Delayed or absent response to mark queries
explanation: The exchange indicates that lack of response to emails, particularly about marks, can prevent students from receiving timely clarification or feedback while the issue is still relevant.
quote: “they never respond to emails” / “that particular course organiser because i knew a few other people had similar problems with their marks.”

explanation: The participant suggests that relying only on questionnaires or surveys is insufficient and expresses a wish for additional ways to provide feedback. This is about feedback mechanisms rather than qualities of academic feedback to students, so it is not directly aligned with the provided feedback-quality themes.
quote: "i wish there were other ways to give feedback, rather than just questionnaires or like surveys"

explanation: The speaker considers the possibility of an automated system for giving feedback, but the comment concerns how students might submit feedback to the institution rather than how the University provides learning feedback to students.
quote: "i feel like an automated thing"

explanation: The participant indicates that feedback may feel more meaningful if it is seen or acted on by higher-level university staff. This relates to institutional responsiveness rather than the characteristics of effective academic feedback to students.
quote: "if it were at a higher level with actual like, higher up, uni, special... looking at something like this"

explanation: The participant suggests students may be more comfortable sharing views when data is collected by other students rather than authority figures. This concerns the research or consultation process, not feedback given to students about their performance.
quote: "students collect data and like, like more comfortable with them, comparing some authority come"
subtheme: Reducing power barriers in feedback collection

explanation: The participant describes excessive university feedback requests causing fatigue and disengagement, with students becoming less willing to participate because requests are too frequent and burdensome.
quote: "university as a whole is asking for far too much feedback all the time. i think people get kind of sick of it... almost every other day about having to these stuff on learn"

code: Lengthy mandatory forms deter specific feedback
explanation: Students feel feedback mechanisms are not accessible when they require many questions to be completed, especially when the student only wants to communicate one specific issue. This makes the process feel inefficient and discouraging.
quote: "why do i have to feel like nine different questions when i only want to give one point across? so i think it deters a lot of people from actually doing the feedback"

explanation: An in-person, low-pressure method of collecting comments at the end of a lecture is presented as more accessible and comfortable, allowing broader participation without overwhelming students.
quote: "as we entered the lecture hall, the lecturer gave up notes and collects them in at the end... a lot of people felt a lot more comfortable to write something down on there"

code: Lack of visible action reduces engagement
explanation: The participant links willingness to provide future feedback to whether previous feedback appears to have been acted upon, suggesting that feedback processes lose value when they do not lead to visible change.
quote: "if there's so many feedback forms... and such little being backed into, like nothing's being acted on that, then it makes you less likely fill the next one"
subtheme: Closing the feedback loop through visible action

explanation: The student suggests that current feedback collection methods mainly attract the same highly engaged students or those with strong complaints, meaning the responses may not represent the wider student population.
quote: "it becomes the same people who answer with the feedback and it's not representative of the university population... the only people that really fill the feedback form is when they either have like, an important complaint, or people that are eager"

explanation: The participant describes being the only person attending online tutorials, but the excerpt does not provide information about the qualities of feedback or how feedback supports learning.
quote: “the last online tutorials. i was the only person there”

explanation: The participant suggests feedback should be read by someone with direct control over the programme, implying feedback is more useful when it reaches a person able to make concrete changes.
quote: “programme director has direct control over how the program's been around.”
subtheme: Feedback Reaches Those with Power to Act

explanation: The participant indicates that if the programme director does not take initiative, feedback should be escalated to someone higher in the hierarchy, reflecting the importance of feedback leading to visible action rather than being ignored.
quote: “if i see that my programme director doesn't really do much, or doesn't take any initiative… perhaps someone who was the main boss”
subtheme: Escalation When Feedback Is Not Acted On

code: Likert and open-ended survey feedback format
explanation: The participant describes a structured survey using Likert-scale satisfaction questions plus an open-ended response box. This concerns collecting students’ opinions rather than feedback given to students about their performance, so it is not directly relevant to the provided feedback-quality themes.
quote: “it's just likert like a scale survey that we get... ‘how satisfied are you?’ ‘what do you think?’ and then, in the end, we get the typeour response, so more open ended.”

explanation: The participant identifies Q&A sessions as the available way to ask questions about course concepts. The excerpt does not provide enough detail about the quality, timing, specificity, or usefulness of feedback received, so it cannot be confidently assigned to a substantive feedback theme.
quote:
primary moderator: “how do you ask questions... q&a session or emailing the lecture or anything?”
s1: “we have a q&a session.”

explanation: Students discuss belonging and departmental connection through student societies rather than feedback from the University; this does not address qualities of good academic feedback.
quote: “i feel a bit more like part of sps, but that's because i've actively chosen to do it… society's kind of go through eusa anyway… it's more our own kind of initiative.”
subtheme: Student belonging outside formal feedback structures

explanation: The comments describe a lack of connection between societies and the School/department, which is about student engagement structures rather than feedback practices.
quote: “we don't have any, like connection to sps at all. it's all through youeusa”
subtheme: Student belonging outside formal feedback structures

explanation: Communication with professors is mentioned in relation to organising talks, not receiving or improving educational feedback.
quote: “we do communicate with professors for talks and stuff. but it's still as more through eusa.”

explanation: The participant suggests that feedback is more useful when students are asked not only what they dislike but also why and how it could be improved, encouraging constructive and usable responses rather than complaints alone.
quote: i always asked, what don't you like, and how, how or why we can improve it.

explanation: The participant gives an example of constructive feedback where students identified that some classes repeated first-year content and suggested targeting the sessions only to direct-entry second-year students. This provides a concrete change that could be implemented.
quote: some students did give suggestions like maybe for some of the classes, they didn't think that it was worth going, because it was just a repeat on first year. so they said, maybe just have it for direct entry. second year students instead of the whole... second year

explanation: The participant distinguishes between feedback that is merely negative or complaint-based and feedback that includes constructive suggestions, highlighting the value of responses that help guide improvement.
quote: so i thought that was a good feedback response. so some of it is constructive. and then some of it’s just complaints.

explanation: The participant suggests that students who attend classes are better positioned to provide constructive feedback about the course structure, while non-attending students may respond carelessly. This concerns perceived quality of survey responses rather than feedback given to students, so it is not directly aligned with the feedback-quality themes.
quote: students who are not attending won't know how bad the structure is going on right now... they will just like fill in... carelessly. then the ones who are actually attending... might fill in more constructively

explanation: The participant identifies long surveys as a barrier to giving feedback, explaining that excessive length reduces motivation and leads to disengagement. This aligns with the need for feedback processes to be user-friendly and not overwhelming.
quote: a barrier, when giving feedback would be, i think the length of the survey, maybe? so like, if it's too long, then i do not want to. like, i'm more likely to just lose interest

explanation: The participant says that a visible progress bar helps them understand how much of the survey remains and encourages completion. This reflects the importance of making the feedback process clear and accessible.
quote: if i do not see the bar in the end, or a bar above, like, to tell me how much i’ve progressed through the survey, that also like, i'm like, ‘how long is it gonna take?’

explanation: The participant values a survey that is short while still allowing them to communicate their point. This suggests feedback mechanisms should prioritise ease of use without removing opportunities for meaningful expression.
quote: a short survey, but also be able to get my point across. i think that's like, you know, yeah

explanation: The participant refers to a video course and an added crash course video on YouTube as part of learning resources, but this does not directly describe feedback from the University or qualities of effective feedback.
quote: because we have a video course as part of learning resources. i've added a crash course video to youtube

explanation: The participant suggests that an aggressive manner is unlikely to lead to change, implying that feedback or communication needs to be delivered in a way students can receive and use rather than in a hostile or overwhelming tone.
quote: it was really aggressive. and then like, i just don't think that's the kind of way that any change is actually gonna happen.

explanation: The participant suggests feedback should be provided before problems become consequential, rather than only after an exam when students are already anxious and cannot use it to improve their performance.
quote: “i wonder if there’s a way to have feedback like, before it's a problem... we have the feedback after exams... a lot of us were very worried about the exam... it wasn't until after the exam and the feedback session that suddenly they were made aware”

explanation: Feedback occurring only after the exam is perceived as having limited value because the issue had already affected students’ preparation and experience.
quote: “we have the feedback after exams... it wasn't until after the exam and the feedback session that suddenly they were made aware of how everyone was just like, terrified.”

explanation: The participant notes that the same issue had been raised by a previous cohort, implying that feedback needs to lead to visible changes across cycles rather than being collected without timely action.
quote: “it was a feedback that was given by last year as well... last year had the same feedback about that specific thing... it just takes a while for the change to happen”
subtheme: Closing the feedback loop across cohorts

explanation: The participant argues that when feedback concerns teaching quality or course delivery, the university should respond more quickly so that educational standards improve in time to benefit current students.
quote: “when it's related to the course, the level of education should be a lot quicker. and that was just the draw back of some of the stuff.”

explanation: The participant describes concern that using the formal university complaints route would remove anonymity and leave complainants feeling unprotected. This relates to grievance handling rather than educational feedback to students, so it is not thematically relevant to the provided feedback themes.
quote: “whatever we say to them, like as complaints, will no longer remain anonymous… we as like victims, in this case, we won't have protection for what was done to us”

code: No visible change after student feedback
explanation: The participant describes repeatedly being asked for feedback by departments but not seeing clear action or improvement as a result, suggesting a missing feedback loop where information is collected but not visibly used.
quote: “they keep asking us how they, how they can improve their work, improve their job responsibility. but, you know, i have the same feeling, kind of, not seeing the change or not seeing the obvious change in those departments.”

explanation: Students are unsure who receives or reads course feedback, indicating a lack of transparency in the feedback process and reducing confidence that their comments are reaching the relevant people.
quote: “i’m not entirely sure. probably it could be the professors... i have no idea who will be seeing it.”

code: Feedback should reach those able to act
explanation: The participant argues that course organisers should have priority access to course feedback because they are responsible for the course and therefore best placed to use the information for improvement.
quote: “course organizers should have the priority to see this feedback because they are the ones who are organizing the whole course. but if they're not seeing it... they won't be that helpful”

code: Need transparency about who receives feedback
explanation: The participant suggests that feedback forms should explain where feedback goes and who will use it, making the process clearer for students.
quote: “it would be good if all of the ones that are teaching would get that feedback. so i was thinking that maybe more transparency, that aspect could also help.”

explanation: The participant notes that while students may want to know who receives their feedback, too much visibility may reduce honest responses if students fear being identified or treated differently.
quote: “there's got to be a midpoint between transparency and also confidentiality. making sure that those answers are surely confidential... we feel it's, yeah, like a bit harsh, or they'll treat us differently.”

explanation: The participant frames feedback as information that should lead to concrete improvement in a course or learning experience, rather than being merely evaluative.
quote: “i drew a student or individual giving a piece of feedback back to a lecturer or another student, and then this lecturer or student makes improvement of their course. and then the other students are happy.”
subtheme: Closing the feedback loop through change

explanation: Feedback is understood as part of a process of moving forward and improving the university experience, implying value when it contributes to development over time.
quote: “you can sort of see it as a way of improvement, yeah. yeah. to move forward in terms of university.”

explanation: The excerpt only contains procedural closing remarks and does not discuss student feedback or its qualities.
quote: "thank you very much for coming." / "i should stop the recording."

explanation: The excerpt only contains participants identifying their names and programme/year of study, with no discussion of feedback practices or qualities of good feedback.
quote: i’mg5bs2, i'm a fourth year student studying veterinary medicine. / g5bs1, fourth year veterinary medicine student as well.

explanation: The participant describes a feedback-related interaction as annoying and unhelpful because it was delivered with a hostile attitude, but the extract does not clearly relate to feedback provided to students by the University or to one of the specified feedback quality themes.
quote: "it was kind of like really annoying, not helpful... they go to like the people who are running the course with the attitude of like, we hate you."

explanation: The participant suggests feedback is more likely to have impact if it comes directly from those experiencing the issue, rather than being filtered only through programme directors.
quote: feedback should be more impactful as well... if it comes from the people who are directly receiving it, it would also make that much easier. so that's another, having access to like the higher ups.

code: Need for transparent feedback escalation routes
explanation: The participant expresses uncertainty about how feedback moves through university levels and wants clearer understanding of communication between programme-level staff and higher-level decision makers.
quote: i just wonder what the level, what it's like at the higher levels... may mean, like, like our course director... having a better communication with the school director or something like that... because we know nothing at all.

code: Feedback framed as strengths and weaknesses
explanation: The participant describes feedback as identifying strengths and weaknesses, but notes that when there are no perceived weaknesses, they feel little motivation to engage in the feedback process.
quote: your feedback is like you give their strengths and weaknesses. but because i never really found any weaknesses, i never really had the motivation to like, give feedback.

explanation: The participant describes receiving a prompt to evaluate service immediately after a bank interaction. This concerns customer feedback collection rather than educational feedback to students, so it is not thematically relevant to the provided feedback-for-learning themes.
quote: “after i went out of the bank, i received a text asking, how was his service?”

code: Frequent feedback solicitation for minor encounters
explanation: The participant notes that feedback requests are increasingly common after small or everyday interactions, including university events and coffee places. This relates to feedback collection practices rather than qualities of effective academic feedback.
quote: “it's quite common, and more like, more and more nowadays, for any kind of, like little encounter… they sent an email, like, how was this?”

explanation: The participant describes posters encouraging customers to provide feedback in exchange for a possible reward. This is about soliciting consumer feedback, not feedback given to students to support learning.
quote: “a lot of posters saying like, give us feedback, like win a free lunch or something… on all the tables of the cafes.”

explanation: The participant frames feedback as serving an improvement function, enabling lecturers or the institution to adjust the course so that it is better for future students rather than remaining unchanged year to year.
quote: , the purpose is obviously to make the course better. so it's not the same as last year.

explanation: The participant links feedback to improved student outcomes, suggesting that effective feedback should help students do better academically and improve their performance.
quote: and so it benefits the students too, in order to for them to do well in their academic career... it makes students better to perform.

explanation: The participant describes unclear or contradictory institutional identity cues, with the veterinary school required to use the wider university logo while students do not feel connected to the main university. This is not directly about academic feedback quality, so it is coded as undefined.
quote: “we have to use the edinburgh uni’s logo . but we don't feel like part of the main uni. so i guess it'd be quite nice to just have some like, obvious line of like, obvious connections.”

explanation: The participant criticises feedback and decision-making systems as overly complex and difficult to understand, suggesting that students cannot see why requested changes are blocked or delayed. This relates to the need for feedback systems to be clear and transparent.
quote: “all the feedback systems are so complex, i can understand why we need some level of complexity. but when there are things that you can see are wrong. and there's still nothing being changed of it for some stupid political reason”
subtheme: Transparency of feedback systems and decision-making

explanation: The participant states that over-complex processes mean changes take years to happen, reducing the perceived value of giving feedback because action is not timely.
quote: “don't over complexify that it takes years for anything to actually happen.”

code: Lack of action following student survey
explanation: The participant reports that even after a student survey showed strong demand, the requested change did not happen. This reflects feedback not being acted upon, limiting its usefulness in producing improvement.
quote: “even though we did a student survey and there was such a high demand to just it, now we don't have it”
subtheme: Closing the feedback loop through visible action

explanation: The participant suggests that students should be able to feed back before exams about topics they feel underprepared for. This highlights feedback being valuable when provided before the assessment, while there is still time for staff or students to respond.
quote: “it maybe quite a good way to have some way of feeding back before exams, especially for things that you're worried about.”

code: Feedback loop before and after assessment
explanation: The participant imagines raising concerns before an exam and then later checking whether those concerns were reflected in performance. This suggests a cyclical process where feedback is gathered, reviewed, and used to inform future teaching or learning.
quote: “before you go in… ‘i don't think i know this.’ and then like, then later you can be like, yeah, i see that.”

explanation: The participant describes the size of the class and the number of mature students, but this does not relate to the quality, delivery, clarity, timing, or usability of feedback.
quote: “i think we're about i don't know, 250? or something like that? it is a big group… mature, we're only like five?”

explanation: The participant describes feedback practices as inconsistent across courses and settings, with effectiveness depending on class size and context.
quote: i think sometimes, yes, sometimes, no, it depends on the context, like, in my experience has been quite varied.

explanation: Having both a form and in-lecture discussion was seen as useful because different students feel comfortable using different modes of communication.
quote: they had a form that we could fill in, and the other one... they also asked for feedback in the lecture... at least having those options because some people do feel more comfortable like just saying things directly to the lecturers.

explanation: The participant indicates they would not have spoken in a non-anonymous lecture setting and preferred the form, suggesting anonymity makes the feedback process more accessible and comfortable.
quote: i know i wouldn't have said anything because obviously that way, it's not anonymous. so i just filled out the form.

explanation: The lecturer discussed the feedback results the following week, which made the process feel responsive and helped students see that their input had been considered.
quote: the following week like they did, she like discussed pretty much the results from the lecture and also from feedback as well.
subtheme: Rapid closing of the feedback loop

explanation: Even though changes were not made, the participant valued that staff reviewed and addressed the main points, making the feedback process visible and transparent.
quote: they didn’t really change anything, but like, at least like they showed they had taken that into account... they listen and they like, go through the results and stuff because they like pretty much addressed all of the main points.

code: Feedback without change has limited value
explanation: The participant distinguishes between acknowledgement and actual action, implying that feedback is more effective when it leads to concrete changes or improvements.
quote: as much as when i say like, they don't really do anything, they didn’t really change anything

code: Small classes enable students to feel heard
explanation: The participant felt that in a smaller class most students could contribute and be included, making the feedback process feel more meaningful.
quote: because of the smaller class, i feel like practically everyone or most people probably, like had a say either like in the lecture or the form. and you're like, we're kind of included that way.

explanation: In larger courses, the participant felt that feedback systems did not capture or respond to the full range of student concerns, reducing trust in the process.
quote: in a lot of our larger courses, it feels less like, we can all like we're all being heard... each year group is massive. and a lot of the time, it feels like they're only focusing on certain courses, or certain like groups of people

code: Narrow focus misses wider student concerns
explanation: The participant notes that recurring attention to dissertation feedback meant issues in other courses were not being recognised, suggesting feedback should reflect the full range of relevant goals or concerns.
quote: they usually, like reference feedback that had to do with like our disertations... but... the other courses that we're doing that like, you know, raising issues about. that's not really being like seen

explanation: The participant reports being discouraged from posting feedback because course organisers can see names, especially given their distinctive name and fear of developing a reputation.
quote: they can still see your name, like the course organizers. and i know that that's definitely put me off, like saying stuff... my name is very unique... i don't want to like get a rep so to speak.

explanation: The participant describes being told not to expect essays to be marked by a certain date, indicating concern about delayed return of assessment feedback and its impact on students.
quote: "don't expect me to mark all of your essays before this date"

explanation: The participant reports staff using offensive language in emails and explanations to students. This concerns the tone and accessibility of university communication, though it is only indirectly related to feedback quality.
quote: "telling him that the school are assholes, like he would explicitly swear or use offensive words"

explanation: Students describe uncertainty and perceived unfairness around whether missed classes, strike participation, or covered content will affect assessment marks, suggesting unstable or unclear assessment standards.
quote: "if we had like any sort of assessment, kind of covering the topics that were covered on certain classes... because we were supporting the strike, we're going to be marked down"

explanation: The participant explains that essay questions could be withdrawn shortly before the deadline, after students had already worked on them, making guidance too late to be useful and undermining students’ ability to complete the assessment effectively.
quote: "they get like, an email two weeks before the deadline: ‘oh, you cannot do this question anymore’... 'i've been working on it for like the past semester'"

code: Perceived unfairness in changing assessment options
explanation: The decision to remove essay questions linked to strike-affected teaching is viewed as unfair because students may have already independently researched those topics, indicating concern about inconsistent application of assessment rules.
quote: "they decided, ‘oh, you cannot do those essays, questions, because that was during this strike’... 'it’s kind of unfair'"

code: Low likelihood due to time burden
explanation: The participant describes being unlikely to provide feedback because the process feels too time-consuming and demanding, particularly when asked to write extended open-text responses. This concerns barriers to completing feedback rather than qualities of feedback provided to students, so it is not directly aligned with the specified feedback-quality themes.
quote: “in my head the probability is literally nothing… there's no one that really has the time… ‘in your own words, please, can you say/ explain why you have this experience?’ i don't want to write like that much.”

explanation: The student describes completing a scheduling feedback/request form, but the response does not reflect the information they provided. This suggests a lack of transparency because the learner cannot see how their input affected the outcome.
quote: “they asked you to list like what times you can and can't do... they send you back like a list of options. and it's all the ones that you can't attend. that you already told them about. and it's yeah, it's frustrating.”
subtheme: Visibility of how student input is used

explanation: The form is described as awkward and involving many steps, making the process difficult to navigate and not user-friendly.
quote: “it's like it's really weirdly put up form. and you do all of the little steps.”

code: Responsiveness affects willingness to give feedback
explanation: The student indicates that giving feedback in person feels acceptable only when the recipient is willing to listen and genuinely wants to hear students’ views. This reflects the importance of feedback being received in a way that is accessible and supportive to the learner.
quote: “it also depends on the kind of person we've given the feedback to, because if they're willing to listen, and actually want to hear us, that's fine.”

code: Fear of repercussions from giving feedback
explanation: The student reports concern that giving personal feedback to an unsympathetic staff member could negatively affect them later in classes. This is relevant to the broader feedback environment but does not directly map onto the provided principles of good feedback to students.
quote: “we kind of will not give a personal feedback, just because we all fear how it's going to impact on us... there might be some repercussions.”
subtheme: Psychological safety and protection from repercussions

explanation: The participant links smaller class sizes and tutorials/seminars with more personal, interactive engagement, suggesting these settings make it easier to receive and discuss feedback.
quote: “there are just four tutorials and seminars… the lecturers are the tutors for each one of those… it always feels much, much more personal and sort of interactive and engaging… every tutorial will be relatively small. and then sort of getting feedback there/ discussing a paper there”

explanation: Feedback is described as occurring through discussion of a paper in tutorials, indicating a feedback process where students can engage with comments and improve understanding through dialogue.
quote: “every tutorial will be relatively small. and then sort of getting feedback there/ discussing a paper there, for instance”

explanation: The student describes receiving assessments back with information on how many points were awarded, which makes performance evidence visible, though it may be limited if not accompanied by qualitative guidance.
quote: “for math ones, we also got the assessments back… how many points we got”
subtheme: Clear marking criteria and performance breakdown

explanation: Essay submissions are returned with a grade and a paragraph of written feedback, providing more detailed information than a mark alone and potentially helping students understand their performance.
quote: “my sps courses are online with the essays… they always come back with obviously the grade and then a whole paragraph of written feedback sometimes”

explanation: The participant values focus-group style discussion but wants it directed toward specific course staff or decision-makers who can implement changes, rather than only discussing shared experiences with other students.
quote: "i want something that i actually feel like will make a big difference. like something like this but where you're actually talking to the specific with the course."

code: Peer discussion perceived as limited influence
explanation: The participant suggests that speaking mainly with other students may feel less useful because students often share similar experiences and may not have the authority to act on the issues raised.
quote: "i feel like saying this to other students, like i think we probably all have had very similar experiences... i want to speak specifically to people who... can really impact"

explanation: The speaker identifies focus groups as a potentially good way to gather feedback from students, though this refers to students giving feedback to the university rather than feedback given to students about their learning.
quote: "this is almost a good way of getting feedback, because you could do it with a focus group"

explanation: The student describes the student-staff committee occurring too late in the semester, meaning issues encountered early could not be addressed promptly. This reflects the importance of feedback being gathered and responded to while there is still time to act.
quote: the student staff committee, which only ended up happening like about the sixth or seventh week of the semester... some problems that kind of i encountered early on, could be resolved early on, which was a little bit annoying.

explanation: The student reports that staff behaviour made students feel their feedback was unwelcome, which undermines an accessible and psychologically safe feedback process.
quote: he kind of said, 'why are you here? you have a lecture now?'... i thought that was quite bad... just trying to be like, we don't want to hear your feedback.
subtheme: Welcoming and psychologically safe feedback channels

explanation: The student attempted to make feedback usable by organising it into subsections and proposing solutions, suggesting that actionable feedback benefits from clear identification of issues and practical ways forward.
quote: i took everyone's feedback, i compiled it into subsections, and then into solutions that i thought were appropriate.

explanation: The student felt some feedback was rejected through broad criticism rather than being engaged with constructively. This contrasts with actionable feedback, which should specify behaviours or changes rather than dismissing concerns.
quote: a lot of them got kind of shut down very quickly. but it's basically saying, oh, you're just lazy.

explanation: The student gives a concrete example of feedback about catch-up materials needing to be released earlier so direct-entry students could prepare before lectures began.
quote: this needs to be released earlier because for direct entry students... they released the catch up course after freshers week when we actually started... i could have got them a week before i came to uni and then had enough time to get through it

explanation: The student notes that some feedback was accepted, minuted, and resulted in a new course, showing a feedback loop where information led to a concrete improvement.
quote: they kind of they accepted openly and minutes were taken and some bits have been implemented. i mean there's an implemented new course on how to use some software we have to use which was quite good.
subtheme: Closing the feedback loop through visible change

explanation: The student felt uncomfortable giving honest feedback about a staff member in front of that person, suggesting that the feedback environment was not transparent or accessible enough to enable frank evidence-based discussion.
quote: i felt quite uncomfortable to raise the issues about this member of staff... i thought it was like a really awkward position to put people in to have to say it in front of them.

explanation: Another participant identifies a conflict of interest in having the staff member present when feedback about them is being discussed, suggesting the need for clearer procedures to make feedback processes reliable and fair.
quote: i feel like there's definitely a conflict of interest there, which is something that should be like codified, like not having that be an issue.

explanation: The student suggests that feedback should happen more frequently rather than only at a required point in the semester, indicating the value of repeated opportunities to receive and use feedback.
quote: make it more frequent, to be able to give feedback. because we don't have like the weekly thing we're using.

explanation: The student indicates that waiting until a mid-semester or end-of-summer point is too delayed, and that the time before feedback is provided should be shortened.
quote: give it like mid semester, like at the end of summer, but then shorten the time, maybe

explanation: The student describes needing to actively seek out feedback through Piazza, which made them less likely to engage with it. This suggests feedback was not integrated into an accessible ongoing cycle.
quote: so it's either you go out of your way to make that feedback, which is on piazza. and when i realized that it was the class, i was like, i'm not doing this.

explanation: The participant discusses finding community and identity through societies rather than within their course or school, particularly due to limited in-person interaction during COVID. This does not relate to qualities of effective feedback, so it is coded as Undefined.
quote: "i think those are more places where you find community and where you have other students around you, especially with covid. i think last year with lectures online, i didn't really... i wasn't able to meet other people in my course because of that. so, yeah, i think the community kind of makes what your identity is, in your location."

explanation: The student notes that a course explained how feedback systems work, suggesting that transparency about the feedback process can make feedback more meaningful and useful, particularly for engaged students.
quote: "it was an anthropology course on audit culture. so it was about the feedback. so they were kind of explaining the mechanism behind it... if you're super interested, that would have been, i think, a useful insight."

code: Informal complaints not converted into formal feedback
explanation: The student describes discussing course problems with peers but not escalating them through formal feedback channels. This is relevant to the broader feedback process but does not directly describe qualities of effective feedback to students.
quote: "we’ll complain to each other, but like not escalate it any further."

explanation: The participant wants structured opportunities for students to discuss course strengths and weaknesses with organisers so that courses can be changed in future.
quote: "having like, a proper sit down with the course organiser at the end of semester, to maybe like, sort of discuss how courses can be changed in the future, and what things worked and what didn't."

explanation: The participant suggests focus groups at the end, and possibly beginning, of each course to gather student feedback and use prior student experiences to inform course delivery.
quote: "having a focus group for each course, at the end of that course. and maybe even at the beginning of the course, to see how students worked with previous voices. and like having that be implemented"

explanation: The participant emphasises openness about how student feedback is handled, including sharing meeting minutes so students can see what happens after feedback is collected.
quote: "proposing some sort of very open transparency in terms of how, how the feedback is being treated... having those minutes, like parts of the minutes shared with the student body so that we know what's going on in those meetings"

explanation: The participant suggests making feedback directly available to the school welfare body, implying that some feedback may relate to student wellbeing or issues with lecturers; however, the point is incomplete and its relevance to feedback quality is unclear.
quote: "also, i think having feedback made available directly to the welfare body of the school, because i do not like with certain lecturers, definitely the people, some students would like to...."

explanation: The participant says feedback is more valuable when the institution explicitly reports what was said and what actions will be taken, making the impact of student feedback visible and transparent.
quote: “i've never really had the thing immediately they get back to you being like, okay, so because so many of us said this, this is this, this school has decided to focus back on this, this and this. and i feel like that would be really helpful because then you actually know that what you're saying actually has an impact”

explanation: The participant describes submitting feedback forms as ineffective because there is no observable response or evidence that the feedback has been considered or acted on.
quote: “most of the time, i feel that even if i feel it feedback... it literally is just like sending the form back into the void and nothing ever happens.”

code: Vague response to feedback limits usefulness
explanation: The participant notes that a lecturer mentioned receiving feedback but did not clearly explain what the feedback was or how it informed changes, reducing the usefulness of the response.
quote: “one of the lecturers has started teaching in a slightly different way and they did vaguely say that they had some feedback or something. it's not really helped much”

explanation: The participant wanted specific improvements to be made but perceived the response as dismissive and insufficiently concrete, suggesting that feedback needs to lead to clear actions for improvement.
quote: “i was like, you really need to do all of these things better. but then they gave up very vague like, oh, so people said, maybe it'd be better if we wrote on a piece of paper and rejected that.”

explanation: The participant indicates that there is no specific tutor or assigned person within the advisory system, suggesting a lack of structured, continuous point of contact for guidance or feedback.
quote: “you can talk...there's no tutor there.”
subtheme: Lack of consistent point of contact

explanation: The participant describes a classmate being asked to provide feedback on a university service even though the original problem had not been resolved. This suggests that feedback processes are perceived as ineffective when they are not part of a cycle where concerns lead to action and improvement.
quote: “the university didn't really solve it, but they were still asking for feedback… she doesn't think the problem is solved.”

explanation: The example of the printing credit problem highlights that feedback requests may feel inappropriate or unhelpful when the learner cannot see any practical response to previously reported issues.
quote: “she didn't receive the semester’s printing amount… she messaged all the departments she could, but the university didn't actually fix it.”

explanation: The moderator summarises that timing and transparency in giving feedback have emerged as useful points for making recommendations to the university.
quote: “we've heard something… about the timing and about the transparency in terms of giving feedback. and that's really useful for us to make suggestions to the university.”

explanation: The student describes a structured pattern of personal tutor contact, with additional availability when needed, indicating feedback/support as an ongoing process rather than a one-off event.
quote: every semester, i think three times a year but she's quite nice. she said anytime any time you need her just send her an email and she will meet me as soon as possible.

explanation: Staff contacted the student quickly after they failed an assessment, suggesting feedback or support was most useful when provided promptly while the issue was still current.
quote: when i fail my animal body 2 last december... several staff, including my pt and the year administrators think i really need a hand and got in touch with me immediately.

explanation: The student contrasts previous experiences of feeling judged with a supportive personal tutor interaction, highlighting the importance of feedback being communicated in a way that feels approachable and emotionally safe.
quote: i took all my courage to say...to tell her my difficulties. and yeah, she was so nice. she didn't judge me and she was really kind

explanation: The tutor provided suggestions after discussing the student’s difficulties, indicating feedback that helped the student identify ways forward rather than simply noting failure.
quote: she was really kind, really very well helping me. give me suggestion about everything.

explanation: Another student states that feedback has not meaningfully occurred during the year, indicating an absence of an ongoing feedback process.
quote: really, there’s no feedback has really gone into this year.

explanation: The participant describes cancelling student accommodation due to COVID-related lack of in-person classes and currently commuting to university. This provides background context but does not relate to qualities of good feedback.
quote: "i cancelled it because there was no point of me staying in year one for covid... i didn't have any more in person classes. so i just went back home." / "no, . i actually commute to university this year."

code: Desire for greater mental health curriculum coverage
explanation: The participant expresses dissatisfaction with the course content and suggests that classes should include more coverage of mental health. This relates to course content rather than the quality or characteristics of feedback, so it is not thematically relevant to the provided feedback themes.
quote: "i think we need classes covered in more mental health... i think that part of the course is not disappointed me."
subtheme: Out of scope: curriculum content concerns

explanation: The participant identifies focus groups as an effective format because they allow students to express views more freely and feel heard. This relates to student voice processes rather than feedback on academic performance, so it is not directly aligned with the provided feedback-quality themes.
quote: "i think focus group would be the most effective... at least we are given the opportunity to..." / "yeah. about expression, like definitely the focus group."

explanation: The moderator frames a contrast between a safe focus-group environment and situations where staff say they will consider student views but may dismiss them. This concerns perceived responsiveness to student voice, not specific formative feedback on learning goals or performance.
quote: "you feel like it's a safe space where you can, like, express your views and that they are heard... as compared to... them then just saying ‘we'll take it into account’ or dismissing it"

code: Uncertainty about how input will be used
explanation: The participant expresses uncertainty about what will happen with the focus-group data, and the moderator explains the process of aggregating responses into a report and toolkit. This is about transparency of the research process rather than feedback to students on their academic work.
quote: "i'm not sure how this is going to work" / "we'll pull all of them together... create a report and a toolkit based off of that"

code: Society discussions create camaraderie but unclear impact
explanation: Students describe using societies as spaces to discuss issues and build a sense of shared concern, but they are uncertain whether these conversations lead to meaningful change or formal feedback outcomes. This does not directly address qualities of good academic feedback, so it is coded as undefined.
quote: “through the societies, you can have the conversations, i don't know if they go anywhere though, or if they actually incite change, but it does bring that sense of camaraderie about an issue.”
subtheme: Informal Peer Spaces for Shared Concerns

code: Informal society relationships affect discussion dynamics
explanation: The student notes that knowing society members more personally than lecturers changes the nature of conversations. This relates to informal communication context rather than specific characteristics of effective university feedback.
quote: “we're talking with them, and you know these people like much more intimately than, say your lecturer. so i think that's what changes the dynamics.”
subtheme: Informal Peer Spaces for Shared Concerns

explanation: The student feels the University is seeking feedback on a superficial issue rather than on matters that would improve the service. This suggests feedback processes should be aligned with meaningful goals and actual student needs.
quote: “what the change of name looks like, that's not the most important thing… do you have like more important things to attend to rather than ‘should we name ourselves inclusion services?’”

explanation: The participant argues that changing terminology will not improve the service unless the University focuses on what it actually does, implying feedback should lead to meaningful improvement rather than cosmetic changes.
quote: “if you do not kind of like, focus on what you're actually doing the changing of name won’t solve any problems.”

explanation: The student notes that the disability service repeatedly sent the same feedback form, which may indicate a burdensome or poorly prioritised feedback process rather than one that is useful to students.
quote: “whether to change their name from a disability service to something else… they kept repeatedly sending it as well.”

code: Feedback demonstrates respect for student input
explanation: The participant frames effective feedback processes as those that show students their views are valued and can improve the educational experience.
quote: i feel like an effective one can show like how students are respected, like the school values our input and try to make the next cohort better.

code: Address current cohort concerns in real time
explanation: The student argues that feedback should not only benefit future cohorts but should be acted on while current students are still experiencing the course issue.
quote: while it's nice to make sure that the next cohort gets a better experience, if from day one, there's a problem or if we’re having a problem, that should be addressed for the current cohort.

code: Continuous feedback channels throughout the course
explanation: The participant wants an accessible feedback space available from the start to the end of the course, enabling concerns to be raised and addressed as they emerge.
quote: just having avenues for consistent feedback, maybe even like every week, not necessarily a survey every week, but like a space for feedback that's present fromweek one to the end of the course to address students concerns as they are happening in real time

explanation: The participant describes repeated student complaints about assessment conditions being ignored over many weeks, undermining trust in the feedback process.
quote: many students immediately complained – imknow that for a fact,, and the complaints from week one actually were dismissed consistently for the past eleven weeks have been dismissed.
subtheme: Failure to close the feedback loop

code: Need for feedback beyond individual lecturer control
explanation: The student suggests that important course concerns should involve additional bodies rather than depending solely on one lecturer’s decision-making.
quote: have that also be beyond the lecture to a point, like have other bodies involved in trying to make that because like, something as simple as a formula booklet should not be left to the jurisdiction of one lecturer.

explanation: The phrase 'take this into account' is experienced as frustrating because it does not clearly communicate what will change or when, making the feedback response feel ineffective.
quote: they said, ‘okay, we will take this into account, but it will not happen this semester’. because they said, it was already set up with it. yes, sometimes the phrase like ‘take this into account’ makes me feel very annoying. because what does it mean? like they won't do anything.

code: Delayed change reduces usefulness of feedback
explanation: Students are told their concern may be considered but not implemented in the current semester, limiting the usefulness of giving feedback for those affected.
quote: okay, we will take this into account, but it will not happen this semester

code: Lack of standardisation in formula booklets
explanation: The participant highlights the absence of a standardised approach to formula booklets across economics/statistics/econometrics, linking this to repeated student dissatisfaction.
quote: we hadn't ever seriously considered giving, like, establishing like standardized formula booklets for economic students and like statistics and econometrics

explanation: The participant indicates that students have consistently raised the formula booklet issue over multiple cohorts, but it has not been meaningfully considered or addressed.
quote: that's like something that students have consistently complained about, since classes have moved back in person.

explanation: The student describes having to repeatedly contact multiple people and escalate to senior staff to get any action, suggesting an ineffective process where feedback/queries are not handled efficiently or clearly.
quote: “this ‘going around in circles’ thing has been just a very, like, repetitive thing that's been happening. i ended up having to contact the provost to get anything done about my appeal.”

explanation: The student identifies confusion about whether their issue belongs to complaints or appeals, with each route redirecting them elsewhere. This reflects a lack of transparent, accessible guidance about how concerns should be addressed.
quote: “they were like, oh, well, why don't you speak to complaints about that? thing is, i had actually submitted a complaint twice. however, they were like, oh, this is actually the appeals jurisdiction, so we actually can't do anything.”

explanation: The student explicitly asks for a framework to prevent similar problems from recurring, indicating a need for stable processes and shared criteria so future cases are handled reliably.
quote: “in the future, can we find some way to do some sort of framework in order to just prevent this whole situation from ever occurring again?”

code: No response after asking what to do next
explanation: After being told they cannot submit a complaint, the student asks what they should do and receives no further response. This highlights the problem of delayed or absent feedback when timely guidance is needed.
quote: “then i was like, okay, that's awesome. but then what am i supposed to do? and i have not been responded to since.”

code: Dismissive handling of missing exam submission
explanation: The student reports that staff minimised the significance of an exam not being submitted or graded, leaving the student without clear evidence-based explanation or meaningful information about the impact of the issue.
quote: “they were kind of basically saying it was not their fault that they hadn't submitted those exams... they just were like, yeah, doesn't really matter anyway.”

explanation: The student describes different support services and staff members not knowing what to do or how to advise them, suggesting inconsistent communication and lack of shared understanding across the institution.
quote: “it just seems like nobody knows anything about what we're supposed to be doing. they didn't know anything. spoke to my personal tutor. he was like, oh, have you spoken to sso, i've got no clue.”

explanation: The student perceives that different parts of the institution do not communicate with one another, producing fragmented guidance rather than a coherent feedback or support process.
quote: “it just feels like there's no connection in between them... none of them actually speak with one another.”

explanation: Senior staff reportedly acknowledged that the situation was serious but did not know what to do, indicating a lack of reliable criteria or procedures for responding consistently to student concerns.
quote: “they were like, ‘this is really bad, none of us actually know what to do, basically. and we're gonna figure out what we need to do, because they didn't know what to do.’”

explanation: The student directly defines effective feedback as requiring action and a response, not merely passive acknowledgement. This aligns with feedback being useful only when it leads to concrete change or next steps.
quote: “take action, please. there needs to be some kind of response when somebody complains.”

explanation: The student criticises situations where staff say they will look into feedback but then nothing happens, indicating that feedback processes need ongoing follow-up and opportunities for improvement rather than one-off acknowledgement.
quote: “they just are like, okay, we will look into it. and then nothing, after that.”

explanation: The participant describes an administrative survey about an extension as not meaningful or relevant to them, indicating this data segment does not clearly relate to qualities of effective feedback given to students.
quote: “i got a survey when i got like an extension last year. and they were like, how timely did you get your extension and that sort of thing. but, that, i don’t know, wasn’t really relevant. i think i might have filled it out. i didn't care about it.”

code: Weak engagement compared with course feedback
explanation: The participant contrasts the extension survey with course feedback, saying they did not have strong feelings about it. This reflects engagement with surveys rather than a specific feature of effective feedback to students.
quote: “i wasn't that like upset about it like i wouldn't.... like i didn't have strong feelings about it the way that i deal with certain like course feedback.”
subtheme: Limited emotional investment in non-course feedback

explanation: The participant identifies a disconnect when highly experienced professors communicate using professional or technical terminology that students without equivalent background knowledge cannot understand. Good feedback or teaching communication is framed as needing to be expressed in 'students language' at an appropriate level.
quote: "all these professors that have been in the lectures are professionals with 30-40 years of experience... for those who know nothing... some professors do really well, just talking in students language and helping the student learn but some struggle... we don't have 20 years of experience alongside and we can't understand"

explanation: The participant describes uncertainty about how to communicate with the central university, including not knowing who to contact or whether contact is permitted. This relates to institutional communication rather than feedback on student performance, so it does not clearly fit the provided educational feedback themes.
quote: “if it’s related to the main uni, not only do i not know who to email i don't even know if i'm allowed to email”

explanation: The participant contrasts central university uncertainty with clearer local escalation routes within the vet school, naming senior people they could contact if issues became serious. This concerns complaint or representation mechanisms rather than feedback to students on learning.
quote: “i can change stuff on campus if it gets really bad because we have david argyle, we have a few other head people or a uni that will get to contact”

explanation: The participant notes poor engagement with elections, suggesting limited participation in university representation structures. This is not directly about the qualities of effective academic feedback.
quote: “and even for elections no one comes out here...”

explanation: The participant suggests that when issues are already communicated informally through a class representative, they do not feel a need to submit the same feedback through a formal form. This reflects how feedback processes may be unclear or fragmented, with students relying on whether they believe feedback has been visibly passed on or addressed.
quote: “she's the class rep… she got the complaint from me… so i don't feel the need to give feedback on a form… surely we think their class rep would address it. like sticking to just the feedback form as well.”
subtheme: Clear feedback routes and visible ownership

explanation: The participant describes feeling hopeless and less motivated to provide feedback when they do not receive any response, indicating the importance of closing the feedback loop so students know their input has been received and acted upon.
quote: “when sometimes i give feedback and did not hear back from them, i feel hopeless and less motivated to give feedback next time.”
subtheme: Closing the feedback loop sustains engagement

explanation: The participant highlights that a delayed or absent response after giving feedback reduces its value and impact. This suggests that feedback processes should include timely acknowledgement or follow-up while the issue remains relevant.
quote: “i give feedback and did not hear back from them”

code: Lack of institutional accountability to student representatives
explanation: The participant describes student representative structures as existing, but feels the University is not required to listen or respond to the issues raised, making change dependent on individual goodwill rather than formal accountability. This relates to institutional responsiveness rather than feedback to students, so it is coded as undefined.
quote: "we have student representatives... but i think nobody at the university is actually taking into account what they are saying. and because there is no accountability... they don't need to respond... some things have been resolved... but not because they have to."

code: Responsibility for support placed on students
explanation: The participant argues that while student representatives can help, responsibility for addressing student issues should not fall primarily on students; the University should have dedicated institutional support. This concerns governance and student support rather than qualities of academic feedback.
quote: "there are representatives and stuff, but it shouldn't be on the students... there needs to be someone who's at the university."

code: Need for stronger university community and support
explanation: The participant frames the University as a large, fragmented community and calls for something that brings students together and provides meaningful support, rather than perceived performative care. This is not specifically about assessment feedback or learning improvement.
quote: "the university is a large place... it's a community of 40,000 people. there needs to be something that actually brings us together... how do i get support in the community? like, actually. not just, oh, we'll pretend that you know, we care."

explanation: The student describes a negative form of tutor-student interaction where teachers ask questions despite sensing students are uncomfortable or unprepared, and then ridicule them publicly. This suggests feedback or questioning is not communicated in a learner-appropriate, supportive way and may undermine students rather than help them improve.
quote: "they might sort of, like ask the students like kind of questions and stuff, when they actually feel like that the students kind of uncomfortable with answering or the not as well prepared as such, and just kind of like ridiculing them in front of the whole group"

explanation: The comment indicates that public questioning or ridicule can be particularly problematic in SPS when tutorials involve controversial topics, where students may feel more exposed or vulnerable. This relates to the need for feedback and discussion to be handled in a way appropriate to students’ context and experience.
quote: "that can be a big thing in sps, especially with like, controversial topics"

explanation: The participant suggests feedback processes should include space for retrospection or self-reflection immediately after an activity ends, highlighting the value of timing feedback while the experience is still fresh.
quote: "we could allow for some retrospection or self reflection immediately after the end."

explanation: The student reports that module questionnaires close before students receive final assignment feedback, preventing them from evaluating whether that feedback was informative. This indicates a timing problem that limits meaningful reflection on feedback quality.
quote: "sometimes the feedback i forget, we also want to write in the comments that it was informative or was not informative. and we can only do that if the survey closes before we get the final feedback."
subtheme: Alignment of feedback and evaluation timelines

explanation: The student notes that by the time assignment feedback arrives later, they may forget aspects of it or be unable to comment on it effectively, suggesting that delayed feedback loses impact and becomes harder to evaluate or use.
quote: "especially kind of like when we get the feedback on our assignments later on. and sometimes the feedback i forget"

code: Perceived lack of genuine interest in feedback
explanation: The student interprets the awkward timing of questionnaires as suggesting the institution may not genuinely want students to provide feedback. This relates more to perceptions of institutional motives than to the specified features of good academic feedback.
quote: "they need to put the forms out. but they don't really want to get this feedback. or they don't really want answers sometimes."

explanation: The participant suggests replacing long feedback forms with a small number of simple yes/no questions plus optional comments, indicating that feedback processes are more effective when they are easy to complete and not overwhelming.
quote: "more often than not very long feedback forms... most people cannot be bothered to do that... maybe there could be like a more specific one that just has like, three or four yes or no questions. and then optional comments at the end"

code: Separate detailed and quick feedback routes
explanation: The speaker distinguishes between a quick targeted feedback form and a broader open-ended form, suggesting that different levels of detail should be offered depending on the purpose and learner willingness to engage.
quote: "there could be a more open, general feedback forum where people could give more detailed feedback following the course. rather than this specific one, where it's just like this very quick"
subtheme: Flexible feedback routes for different engagement levels

code: Feedback linked to a specific recent change
explanation: The participant describes asking students about whether a newly implemented change worked, which frames feedback against a clear intervention or goal and allows evaluation of whether the action achieved its intended effect.
quote: "we tried implementing this thing until such as this week. do you feel like it worked? yes. no, if you want, give us like additional comments"
subtheme: Evaluating specific changes against intended outcomes

code: In-person open-ended written feedback increases response
explanation: The participant reports that post-it notes distributed during a lecture generated the most feedback, suggesting that feedback opportunities are more effective when they are visible, accessible, and easy to act on in the moment.
quote: "the thing i saw worked best was actually the thing that got by far the most feedback, was when posts posted notes were given out in the final lecture... people sit down and have the whole lecture to write it"

explanation: The supermarket-style smiley/sad-face button example highlights the value of making feedback quick, concrete, and low effort, especially for capturing broad student responses.
quote: "just as you're leaving the hall have like a... smiley face, a sad face... everyone just presses on the way up. like, it just has to make so simple and easy"

code: Detailed forms attract limited student perspectives
explanation: The participant notes that detailed feedback mechanisms only attract some students, implying that overly demanding feedback formats may bias participation and reduce usefulness.
quote: "the fact is, this detailed stuff is only attracting a certain amount of students"
subtheme: Reducing participation barriers and response bias

explanation: The participant describes raising the same problems through student representation over multiple years without apparent change, suggesting a lack of an ongoing improvement cycle where feedback is acted upon and revisited.
quote: “i was a school rep in 2020... i kind of like, brought up those issues like two years ago, but then they will not stop. and then every year is kind of like the similar issues.”

explanation: The staff response appears to dismiss or deflect the student representative’s feedback rather than acknowledge it, limiting its usefulness and discouraging future feedback engagement.
quote: “in the meeting, they said, ‘didn't you not look at the things on the... learn page? ... everything was there’ . and i was like, i didn’t know... i felt very uncomfortable. i tried to collect feedback and give it to you”

explanation: The participant identifies that digital feedback systems may exclude students who do not consistently monitor emails or online systems, making feedback processes less accessible and transparent to all students.
quote: “so much feedback is digitized. students who might not necessarily be keeping up to date as much with emails... might find it more difficult to access that.”

explanation: The participant suggests that impersonal, digitised feedback collection can discourage marginalised students or those with sensitive concerns from contributing, meaning the process may not be accessible or appropriately communicated for all learners.
quote: “marginalised students might feel more uncomfortable, or just generally like less likely to be heard if it's so... digitized and so impersonal... feedback mechanisms”
subtheme: Inclusive and psychologically safe feedback routes

explanation: The participant describes a case where giving feedback about course content and teaching felt inaccessible because the issue was personal and sensitive, indicating that some feedback channels do not support nuanced or difficult feedback effectively.
quote: “a friend of mine who had certain issues... it was very inaccessible, it's very personal. because it's about the course content and how parts of the course was being taught.”
subtheme: Inclusive and psychologically safe feedback routes

explanation: The participant reports that multiple similar surveys are sent within a short time period, which reduces engagement and makes feedback collection feel burdensome rather than useful.
quote: “there are too many surveys... one in week six... after three weeks, or four weeks... they sent out another one, kind of like exactly the same.”

explanation: The participant states that long open-ended survey boxes put students off, while simpler rating-based formats are more successful, highlighting the need for feedback systems to be clear, accessible, and easy to complete.
quote: “the surveys are open ended questions... a big box with a lot of questions. and most of the students will just give it when they look at it... the most successful ones are those with... easier to read, like ratings”

explanation: The participant explains that multiple simultaneous institutional surveys make it harder for student representatives to gather feedback, indicating poor coordination and a lack of manageable, user-friendly feedback processes.
quote: “they kept on sending those long ones, which also made the ones that the students rep made, like hard to get feedback... they have like three or four surveys.”

explanation: The participant suggests a dedicated, accessible place where students can get answers about feedback-related or academic problems, indicating a need for clearer and easier-to-navigate feedback support.
quote: "i would create a hub where things are answered... make a hub that specifically specialises in feedback"
